units.title: Thinking in Compose
units.summary: Compose becomes much simpler once you stop reading it as a new syntax for building View hierarchies. This unit replaces that habit with the three ideas everything else depends on: UI is described from the current state rather than mutated, a composable body is a description the runtime may run again, skip, or discard, and state flows down while events flow up. State ownership, recomposition, effects and performance all assume this model, so it is worth getting right before any Compose API is introduced.

lessons.title: Declarative UI and Why Compose Exists
lessons.summary: What actually changes when a screen is described from its current state instead of created once and mutated afterwards, and why that removes a whole family of synchronisation bugs rather than merely replacing XML with Kotlin.

blocks.text: If you have built Android screens with Views, you already carry a mental model of how UI works. You create a tree of widget objects, usually by inflating an XML layout, you keep references to the ones you care about, and when something changes you call setters on them. Each widget is a long-lived object that holds its own state and exposes getters and setters for it, and your code's job is to keep the properties of those objects matching the application state they are supposed to be showing.

Compose asks you to work the other way round. You do not hold a widget and change it; in fact Compose does not hand you the emitted UI as objects to mutate at all. You write a function that says what the screen should look like for a given set of inputs, and when those inputs change the runtime calls the same function again with the new values and works out what to change on screen. That is the whole of what declarative means here: you supply the description, the runtime performs the update.

rows: Creating the UI
Instantiate or inflate a tree of widget objects and keep references to the ones that will change.
Call a composable function that describes the UI for the current inputs.
Updating the UI
Call setters on the widgets you kept references to.
Call the same function again with new inputs and let the runtime apply the difference.
Where the displayed state lives
Inside each widget, which owns and exposes its own mutable properties.
In the application state the description is derived from; the emitted UI is not exposed for mutation.
What you have to get right
Every code path that changes application state must also update every widget affected by it.
One description that is correct for any state the screen can be in.

blocks.text: The last row is the one that matters. The imperative version makes correctness a property of every transition: each path through the code has to remember every widget that the change affects, and the number of paths grows faster than the number of screens. The declarative version makes correctness a property of one function: given this state, this is the UI. This is a maintainability argument, not a syntax preference, and it is worth being honest about its limits. Describing UI from state does not make state bugs impossible, because the state you compute can still be wrong. What it removes is the narrower and far more common failure where two representations of the same fact drift apart, because one update path knew about a widget and another did not.

A frequent answer is that Compose is declarative because layouts are written in Kotlin instead of XML. That is a language change, not a paradigm change: an imperative widget tree can be built entirely in Kotlin, and plenty of View code does exactly that. What makes Compose declarative is that you never obtain a UI object and mutate it. You provide a function from state to a description of UI, and the runtime decides what has to change.

Take a small profile screen that can be loading, can be showing content, can be showing an error, and has a submit button that is only enabled when the form is valid. In the View version the widgets already exist, so every state change is expressed as a set of mutations against them.

Neither function is wrong on its own. The first is a complete mapping from state to widgets. The second is a second update path, added later for one case, that touches a subset of the same widgets and forgets the rest: the content group is still hidden and the submit button is still disabled, so the screen now shows an error the user cannot act on. Nothing in the code forces the two paths to agree. The widget tree has quietly reached a combination of properties that no single application state describes, and every additional path a screen accumulates adds more of those combinations.

There is now one description of the screen, and every field of the state is read in exactly one place. A failed submission is not a set of widget mutations; it is a new state value with loading false, an error message present and submission enabled again, and the same function produces the matching screen from it. The work has moved rather than disappeared: instead of getting every transition right, you have to model the state well enough that it cannot express a screen you never meant to show. That is why Compose screens usually take one immutable state type rather than a handful of loose flags, and it is a far easier problem to review.

Be able to say what changes, not just to name the two words. Declarative and imperative differ in how an update is expressed: imperative code names the widgets to mutate, declarative code describes the intended result for the current state and leaves the update to the runtime. Compose does not expose the UI it emits for setter-style mutation, so the current state is the only thing driving what is on screen. That is also why Compose fits so naturally with observable state and with unidirectional data flow: once the state is the single input to the UI, giving that state one owner is the obvious next step.

lessons.title: What a Composable Is and How It Executes
lessons.summary: A composable function is not a callback that runs once when you call it. It contributes a description of UI to a Composition the runtime may rebuild, skip or throw away, which is what turns fast, idempotent and side-effect free from advice into a contract.

blocks.text: The usual answer to what a composable is, that it is a function annotated with Composable, is true and explains nothing: it names the syntax that marks the function rather than saying what the function does. The useful definition is about the runtime. A composable runs inside Compose's runtime, and its job is to contribute a description of some UI. It does not return that description to you and it does not draw anything itself; it emits UI into the structure the runtime maintains, which is why a composable normally returns nothing and why it can only be called from another composable.
Three terms are worth pinning down now, because everything later in the Compose path is phrased in them.

items: Composition: the tree of UI descriptions that exists because your composables ran. It is the runtime's record of what your UI currently is, and the only way to change it is by running composables again.
Initial composition: the first run, in which the composables you called are executed and enter the Composition.
Recomposition: a later re-execution, scheduled when state that a composable read has changed, which updates the existing Composition rather than rebuilding it from nothing.

blocks.text: That is deliberately as far as this lesson takes recomposition. How Compose knows which state a composable read, which part of the tree is invalidated by a change, and when a composable can be skipped is a mechanism with its own unit later in this path. What you need here is only the consequence: the body of your function is something the runtime may execute again, on its own schedule, without anyone in your code calling it.

The habit worth breaking early is reading a composable body the way you read onCreate, onResume, or an onClick lambda. Those run because something called them, once per call, in an order you can trace, and the work they perform is the point of calling them. A composable body is a description, and the runtime executes it as often as it needs to in order to keep the Composition current. Four assumptions that are safe for a callback are not safe here.

items: That the body runs once. It runs during initial composition and again on every recomposition that is not skipped.
That the body runs a predictable number of times. How many times depends on what state changed and on what the runtime chose to skip, and that is not part of any contract you can rely on.
That calls to other composables happen in the order they are written, or that a sibling has already run. Compose may execute them in another order, for instance to produce higher-priority UI first.

That every execution reaches the screen. Recomposition is optimistic: Compose expects the inputs to hold still, and if they change again first it can cancel the recomposition and discard the UI it had produced.

blocks.text: Stated positively, the requirement is simple. Running the body again with the same inputs should describe the same UI and do nothing else. It should not also perform an action for a second time merely because the function ran for a second time. A function with that property is called idempotent, and the contract Compose asks for is that composables be fast, idempotent, and free of side effects.

Treating the body as a place where things happen. The reasoning that this code sits in the function, so it runs when the screen appears, is behind most early Compose bugs: an analytics event that fires five times, a request that is sent again on every keystroke, a count that never matches reality. The body is not an event handler. The event is whatever changed the state; the body only says what the screen should look like now.

A side effect is a change that is observable outside the composable's own description of the UI and that happens simply because the body executed. The clearest way to see the problem is a composable that looks entirely reasonable.

Nothing here is invalid Kotlin, and analytics is obviously not forbidden in a Compose app. The problem is that a business event, the user viewed this profile, has been attached to something that is not a business event. That the body of ProfileScreen executed means only that the runtime needed the description: it may happen once, or on every recomposition triggered by an unrelated change nearby, or as part of work that is later discarded. The number your dashboard receives becomes a property of the runtime's scheduling rather than of anything the user did. The same reasoning applies to a counter kept outside the function: what it counts is executions of a function body, which is not a number that means anything to anyone.

The correction is not to move the call somewhere vaguer. It is to attach the work to something that actually happened. Work caused by a user action belongs in the event callback, because an onClick lambda runs once per click and a click is a real event. Work that genuinely belongs to the composition itself, such as starting a load when a screen appears or registering a listener that must later be removed, belongs to Compose's effect APIs, which give that work a defined lifetime tied to the composition instead of to the number of times a function body ran. Those APIs have their own unit later in this path; what matters now is recognising which of the two questions you are answering.
In practice, these are the lines that should make you look twice when you find them written directly in a composable body.

items: Starting a network request, a database read, or any other work that should happen once per event.
Writing to SharedPreferences, DataStore, or a file.
Calling a function on a ViewModel that changes its state.
Sending an analytics or logging event that is meant to count something real.
Registering an observer, listener, or callback with anything outside Compose.
Mutating a variable, collection, or object that is shared with the rest of the app.

blocks.text: This is not a rule that composables may not call functions. Reading parameters, formatting a string, mapping a list into the rows it will show, and calling other composables are all part of describing UI, and repeating them costs nothing but the description. The question to ask about a line is whether running it a second time would do something a second time, or would simply describe the same thing again.

It is worth asking why the runtime demands this, because keep composables pure reads as style advice until you see what it buys. Every mechanism Compose has for making UI updates cheap depends on being free to decide when, whether, and in what order your code runs. Skipping is the obvious one: if the inputs to a part of the tree have not changed, the runtime can leave that part of the Composition alone and not run the function at all, which is only safe when not running it has no consequence beyond not re-describing unchanged UI. Re-execution is the mirror image: the runtime can re-run a scope whenever that is cheaper than tracking a change more precisely, which is only acceptable when running twice costs nothing but the description. Discarding follows from optimistic recomposition, and is only sound when nothing outside the Composition has already acted on the run being thrown away. Ordering freedom is the same argument once more: if execution has no consequence other than the description it produces, the order is the runtime's to choose.

This is also why the guidance is phrased as a forward-looking contract, and it is a detail worth getting right. Compose does not currently execute composable functions in parallel, so claiming that it does is wrong. What the documentation asks is that you write code which would remain correct if it did: no side effects, no dependence on execution order, no assumption that the body of a composable is running on a thread you can reason about. The practical point is not really threading. It is that the number, the timing, and the relative order of executions are the runtime's decisions rather than part of the API you are programming against.

Restricting side effects in composables is not a matter of taste. It is what allows the runtime to skip, repeat, reorder, and discard the execution of your UI description without changing how the app behaves. A composable that carries side effects takes that freedom away, and turns an optimisation the runtime is entitled to make into a bug in your feature.

A strong answer describes the contract rather than the annotation. A composable contributes a description of UI to the Composition; it may run on initial composition, run again on any recomposition, be skipped entirely, run in an order you did not write, or have its work discarded, so correctness must never depend on the body having executed. Side effects therefore belong in event callbacks or in effect APIs with a defined composition lifetime. If parallel execution comes up, the accurate answer is that composables are not run in parallel today and that the requirement is to write code which does not depend on that remaining true.

lessons.title: State Down, Events Up
lessons.summary: Why a Compose screen is built as one owner producing state and children reporting what the user did, what that direction actually buys you, and where the idea stops being a Compose detail and becomes an architectural one.

blocks.text: A composable describes UI from what it is given, which leaves an obvious question: where does what it is given come from, and what happens when the user types something into it? Compose is built around an answer with a direction. State travels down, from whoever owns it to the composables that display it. Events travel up, from the composable where the interaction happened to that owner. Nothing travels sideways, and the composable that renders a value is not the one that changes it.

items: The owner holds the current state and passes it down as parameters.
The composable describes itself from those parameters and keeps no separate copy of them.
The user interacts, and the composable reports what happened by invoking a callback it was given.
The owner interprets that event and decides how the state changes.
The new state flows back down, and the description is produced again from it.

blocks.text: This is called unidirectional data flow because data makes a one-way trip: down as state, up as events, never back and forth through the same channel. The payoff is that exactly one place changes a given piece of state. When a screen shows the wrong thing you do not have to work out which of several components mutated it; you read the owner, and the answer is in one function. The same property is what makes the UI testable, because the thing that produces state can be exercised without any UI at all.

Note that the owner has deliberately not been called a ViewModel. The owner is whoever is responsible for that piece of state, and it might be the parent composable, a plain state-holder class, or a ViewModel when the state is screen-level and has to outlive a configuration change. Choosing between them is a real decision, and it has its own lesson later in this path. The direction described here is the same whichever owner you pick.

An event parameter should say what happened, or what the user asked for. It does not have to mean assign this value to a variable further up. The shape people quote most often is a current value plus an onValueChange callback, and it is the right shape for a component that edits a single value, such as a text field. It is one common pattern, not the definition of the direction: a component whose interactions are actions rather than edits should expose those actions.

ProfileHeader receives the one value it displays and one callback describing the one thing a user can do to it. It owns nothing, it can be previewed or tested by calling it with a string and a lambda, and it can be reused on a screen where editing means something entirely different, because its caller decides what editing does. Compare that with the version almost every codebase grows at some point.

This compiles and renders the same pixels, and it is the most common way the direction quietly disappears. The component now depends on one specific ViewModel type, so it cannot be reused elsewhere, cannot be previewed without constructing that ViewModel, and cannot be tested by passing values in. The deeper cost is that every child holding the ViewModel is another place where state can be read and written, so who changed this stops having a single answer. Passing a ViewModel down the tree is not a shortcut for state down and events up; it is the thing the pattern exists to prevent. Keeping the dependency at one boundary, where a screen-level composable collects the state and hands its children plain data and lambdas, costs a few more parameters and buys back all of the above.

Concluding that unidirectional data flow means every piece of state belongs in a ViewModel. The direction says that each piece of state has one owner and that events travel to that owner. It says nothing about how far away the owner should be. Whether a checkbox, an expanded row, or a scroll position is owned by the composable showing it or by a screen-level holder depends on who else has to read or change it and on how long it needs to survive.

Unidirectional data flow is not something Compose invented, and it is not really a UI-toolkit idea. It is a single rule applied at the scale of a screen: one source of truth for the state, mutation in one place, and everything else deriving what it shows from that. The Android architecture guidance makes the case in three properties worth being able to justify rather than recite. Consistency, because there is one source of truth for what the UI shows. Testability, because the producer of state is isolated from the UI that renders it. Maintainability, because a state change always has a named cause and a single code path. The direction was equally available in the View system, where a ViewModel exposing state that a Fragment observes and renders is the same loop; Compose makes the pattern natural rather than possible, because a composable that describes itself from its parameters is already the render half of it.

The same principle scales into patterns you will be asked about by name: a single immutable state type per screen, user intent modelled as a type rather than a bag of lambdas, and a function that takes the current state plus an event and returns the next state, which is where reducer and MVI-style architectures come from. Those belong to the architecture topic rather than to Compose, and this path deliberately stops at the direction itself.

One term follows directly from all of this and is worth connecting now. When a child needs state that a higher-level owner should control, you move the state up into that owner and pass the current value down with an event callback going back up. That move is called state hoisting, and a child that no longer holds the state is called stateless. How far up to move it, which owner is the right one, and what it costs to hoist further than necessary make up a decision model with its own lesson later in this path.

Expect to be asked why rather than what. Be ready to say what the direction buys: one owner per piece of state so that a change has one cause, children that are reusable and testable because they only receive data and report intent, and a screen that can be reasoned about as a single function from state to UI. Be ready to say that not all state belongs in a ViewModel, and to justify where you would put a specific piece. And be ready to explain why handing a child a ViewModel, or any mutable object it can write to, breaks the pattern even though the screen still looks correct.

units.title: State and State Ownership
units.summary: A declarative UI is only as good as the values it is described from, and Compose will not notice a value changing unless it was told how to. This unit covers what makes state observable, what makes it survive a function running again, what makes it survive the screen being recreated, and who should own it in the first place. It closes on the failure that catches almost everyone once: a collection mutated in place, changing nothing anybody can see. Recomposition, stability and effects all assume this material, so it comes before any of them.

lessons.title: Observable State: `mutableStateOf` and `State<T>`
lessons.summary: Why an ordinary variable can change without anything appearing on screen, what makes a value observable to Compose instead, and why it is the read rather than the write that decides which part of your UI depends on it.

blocks.text: The previous unit left a deliberate gap. A composable describes the UI for the values it is given, and the runtime may run that description again whenever it needs to. What it did not say is how the runtime ever finds out that it needs to. Nothing so far connects a value changing to your description being produced again, and without that connection a declarative UI would simply show whatever it showed the first time.

State, in this context, means any value that can change while the screen is alive and that the screen is described from: a counter, the text in a field, whether a row is expanded, the list of items loaded from the network. The question this lesson answers is what has to be true of such a value for Compose to notice when it changes.

An ordinary Kotlin variable does not qualify. Assigning to a `var` changes the variable and tells nobody, because a plain variable has no mechanism for announcing that it was written. Compose therefore has its own value holder. `mutableStateOf` creates an observable `MutableState<T>`, a single-value holder whose reads and writes the runtime can see.

There are two types because there are two capabilities, and they are worth separating from the start. `State<T>` is a value you can read and observe. `MutableState<T>` adds the ability to write. Handing a composable the read-only type is how you say that it displays this value but does not change it.

The mechanism has two halves, and only one of them is the obvious one. Writing to `value` is the half everyone expects: change the value and the runtime is told. The half that decides how much of your UI is affected is the read. When a composable reads `value` while it is executing, the runtime records that this particular piece of executing code depends on this particular state object. A later write then schedules a recomposition of the code that recorded a read, and of nothing else.

The dependency is created by the read, not by the declaration and not by the write. A composable does not depend on a state object because the object was created nearby or passed in as a parameter; it depends on it because it actually read the value while executing. This one sentence explains most of what the rest of the Compose path is about.

Two consequences follow immediately. Writing the same value again is not a change: the default policy compares the new value to the current one with structural equality, and setting `value` to something already equal schedules nothing. And reading state outside composition — in a click handler, in a coroutine, in a plain function — reads the current value perfectly well but creates no dependency, because there is no executing composable to record one.

How the runtime records those reads and applies those writes is the snapshot system, which is also what makes state changes consistent rather than half-applied. It has its own unit later in this path. Everything in this unit and the next works from the contract just described, without needing the machinery.
The failure that teaches this best is a counter that will not count. It compiles, the click handler runs, the variable really does change, and the number on screen never moves.

Reach for the debugger and you will confirm that `count` becomes 1. That is the confusing part, and it is why the bug survives so long: nothing is broken about the increment. What is missing is the announcement. `count` is a plain `Int` in a plain local variable, so writing it notifies nothing, no composable recorded a dependency on it, and the runtime has no reason to produce the description again. The screen is not stale in the sense of being wrong; it is simply the last description anyone asked for.
Making the value observable is the first correction. It is not yet the whole fix, which is the point of this example.

This version does more than the last one. The body reads `count.value` while it is executing, so a dependency is recorded; the click writes a new value, so a recomposition is scheduled. And the counter still shows zero. The reason is that `mutableStateOf(0)` is a function call inside a function body, so re-executing that body calls it again and produces a brand new holder initialised to zero. The value was observable and the write was seen, but the holder that received the write was discarded and replaced before anything was displayed.

The symptom is worth stating carefully, because it is not always a counter frozen at zero. What is guaranteed is that the value is lost every time the composable that called `mutableStateOf` executes again — it cannot be otherwise, because the holder is created by that call. Whether the reset is immediate or arrives later depends on which piece of code read the value, and therefore on what the write invalidated. Written as above, with the read in the same body, the reset is immediate. Move the read into a lambda passed to another composable and the number can climb normally until something unrelated re-executes the body, at which point it silently returns to zero — the same defect, with a far more confusing symptom. Which code a read belongs to is the subject of the Recomposition unit.

That is exactly the distinction the next lesson exists for: being observable and surviving re-execution are two independent properties, and a working counter needs both. For the rest of this lesson, take the second property on trust — `remember` supplies it — so the observability half can be looked at on its own.

The `by` here is Kotlin's property delegation, not a Compose feature. A delegated property routes reads and writes to another object's `getValue` and `setValue` operators, and Compose defines those for `State` and `MutableState`. The effect is purely notational: `count` now behaves like an ordinary `Int` variable while still being a `MutableState<Int>` underneath, so `count` is a read of `value` and `count++` is a read followed by a write. It needs two imports that are easy to forget, `androidx.compose.runtime.getValue` and `androidx.compose.runtime.setValue`.

rows: Property delegate
`var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`
`count`, `count++`
Almost always. It keeps the call sites free of `.value` noise.
Explicit holder
`val count = remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`
`count.value`, `count.value++`
When the holder itself has to be passed somewhere, so the object rather than the value is the thing you need.
Destructured
`val (count, setCount) = remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`
`count`, `setCount(1)`
When a value and a setter are handed to something separately, which mirrors the value-plus-callback shape hoisting uses.

blocks.text: All three are the same object with the same behaviour, and the choice carries no runtime consequence. Where a real decision does appear is at a composable's boundary. A composable that only displays a value should take the value, not the holder: `fun Badge(count: Int)` can be previewed and tested with a literal and cannot possibly write to anything. Taking `State<Int>` is occasionally the right call and has real consequences for how much of the UI re-executes, which the recomposition unit covers. Taking `MutableState<Int>` hands a child a second write path into state it does not own, which is the pattern the previous unit's lesson on data flow direction warned about.

Reading an assignment to `value` as an instruction that refreshes the screen. It is not a command and nothing is drawn at that moment. It records a new value and marks the code that read the old one as out of date; the runtime decides when to act on that, and may coalesce several writes made in quick succession. The difference matters as soon as you try to write code that assumes the UI has already caught up on the next line.

It is worth being precise about what the runtime records, because the imprecise version — "the composable subscribes to the state" — quietly loses the detail that everything about performance later depends on. The subscription belongs to the region of code that was executing at the moment of the read, not to the function you happen to have written it in and not to the state object's neighbourhood. The runtime's own description of `MutableState` is that reads to `value` during the execution of a composable subscribe the currently executing recompose scope, and that a write schedules recomposition of the scopes so subscribed.

So the same state object read in two places produces two independent dependencies, and moving a read from a parent into a child moves the dependency with it. This is the reasoning the next unit is built on, and it is why "where do I read this?" turns out to be a design question rather than a matter of taste.

The equality behaviour is worth knowing for the same reason. `mutableStateOf` defaults to a structural-equality policy, so assigning a value equal to the current one is not treated as a change and schedules nothing. That is usually what you want and occasionally surprising: a state holding a mutable object can be assigned an instance that is `equals` to the old one and correctly produce no update, even though the object's contents differ from what is on screen. That failure has its own lesson at the end of this unit.

Be ready to explain the counter that does not count, because it is a standard opening and it has two separate causes. A plain `var` is not observable, so nothing is scheduled. A `mutableStateOf` without `remember` is observable, but the holder is recreated whenever the composable that created it executes again, so the value it was carrying is discarded. Then make the point that separates a strong answer: the dependency comes from reading `value` during composition, which is why the location of the read decides how much of the UI a change affects — and, in this case, whether the reset is immediate or turns up later as a value that mysteriously falls back to its initial one.

lessons.title: `remember`: Composition Memory
lessons.summary: Observability and memory are two different properties, and conflating them is behind most early Compose confusion. What `remember` actually stores, why `remember { mutableStateOf(x) }` is the pair you see everywhere, and what a wrong key does to a value that should have changed.

blocks.text: The previous lesson ended on a counter that was observable and still did not count, because `mutableStateOf(0)` sat in a function body that runs again. That is the second half of the problem, and it has nothing to do with observation. A composable body is re-executed, so every local it declares is created afresh, and a value that must outlive one execution needs somewhere to live that is not a local variable.

`remember` is that somewhere. A value computed by `remember` is stored in the Composition during initial composition, and on recomposition the stored value is returned instead of the lambda being run again. The value is forgotten when the composable that called `remember` is removed from the Composition.

Read that as a small cache whose key is a position in the Composition and whose lifetime is the presence of that position. Not a global cache, not a singleton, and not storage that outlives the screen: when the composable leaves — a branch stops being taken, a list item scrolls out of a lazy layout, the screen is navigated away from — the remembered value goes with it.

`remember` and `mutableStateOf` answer two independent questions. `remember` answers "does this value survive my function running again?" and `mutableStateOf` answers "does changing this value tell anyone?" Neither implies the other, which is why the working pattern needs both and why either one alone produces a screen that looks broken in a different way.

`remember` also takes keys. The value is stored with the keys it was computed from, and if any of them change, the next recomposition invalidates the cache and runs the calculation again. Compose compares keys with the class's `equals` implementation. Keys are how you say what the remembered value is a function of, which is the same as saying when it should be discarded.
Because the two properties are independent, there are four combinations, and each of them appears in real code. Being able to predict all four is most of what this lesson is for.

rows: `var count = 0`
No
No

A variable nothing observes. The click really does change it, and it keeps changing — Kotlin's closure captures the variable itself, so repeated clicks accumulate in memory — but no dependency was recorded, so nothing is scheduled and the screen never changes. It returns to its initial value whenever this body executes again.
`val config = remember { loadConfig() }`
Yes
No
A stable value computed once. Correct and common for something that is created rather than changed — a formatter, a `Paint`, a derived constant.
`var count by mutableStateOf(0)`
No
Yes

A write is seen and schedules recomposition, but the holder is recreated at its initial value every time this body executes. Looks like a counter frozen at zero when the read is in the same body; looks like a value that works and then silently resets when the read sits in a lambda that can recompose on its own.
`var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`
Yes
Yes
State a composable owns: it persists while the composable is in the Composition and changing it updates the UI. This is the pair you want almost every time.

blocks.text: The second row deserves more credit than it usually gets. Not everything a composable needs to keep is state: a value that is expensive to construct and never changes wants `remember` and emphatically does not want `mutableStateOf`, because wrapping it in observable state suggests to every reader that something writes to it.
The mistakes that survive review are almost always about keys, and there are two of them pointing in opposite directions. Under-specify and you keep a value you should have discarded.

As long as this composable stays at the same place in the Composition, the remembered holder stays with it. Show a different `user` and the field keeps the previous person's name — or the half-typed edit made to it — because nothing told `remember` that the draft was a function of which user is being edited. Naming that dependency is the fix, and it reads as a statement about the data rather than a workaround.

blocks.code: var draftName by remember(user.id) { mutableStateOf(user.name) }

blocks.text: Over-specify and you get the mirror image. A key that changes more often than the value conceptually does throws the value away for no reason, which for remembered state means the user's input disappears. Keying the draft above on the whole `user` object would do it whenever any unrelated field of `User` differs, and keying it on a fresh object that compares unequal every execution would discard it every time. A freshly created but equal key does not invalidate remember; the comparison is equals, not instance identity.

Reaching for `remember` when the real requirement is that state survives the screen being recreated. `remember` retains a value across recomposition; it does not survive a configuration change, because the Composition itself is not what outlives that. Which mechanism does is the next lesson.

The part of `remember` that is easy to miss is that it has no name. There is no key you supply that identifies the slot; the slot is the call site's position in the Composition. That is why the same line of code can be a different remembered value in each of ten list rows without any of them being confused, and it is also why where you write `remember` matters as much as what you store in it.

Whether that is a bug depends entirely on intent. Discarding a draft when a panel closes may be exactly right; losing it because the panel briefly collapsed during an animation is not. The decision is about lifetime, and the tool for changing the answer is to move the `remember` to a caller that stays in the Composition longer — which is hoisting, two lessons from here.

There is a matching subtlety in what identifies a call site when the same one runs several times, as it does for the rows of a list. Compose has a mechanism for telling those instances apart, and getting it wrong makes remembered state stick to the wrong item after a reorder. That is composition identity, and it has its own unit later in this path; this lesson only needs the fact that `remember` is attached to a position rather than to a name.

The question is usually "what is the difference between `remember` and `mutableStateOf`?", and the weak answer treats them as two ways of doing one thing. Say that they are orthogonal: one gives a value memory across executions, the other makes changes to it observable, and the familiar pairing is a composition of the two rather than an idiom to memorise. Then be ready for the follow-up about keys, where the interesting content is that an under-specified key shows stale data and an over-specified one destroys the user's work.

lessons.title: `rememberSaveable` and State That Must Survive
lessons.summary: Four things a piece of UI state might have to live through — re-execution, leaving the Composition, the screen being recreated, the process being killed — and how to pick a mechanism for a given piece of state without treating saved state as a database.

blocks.text: "Does this state survive?" is not one question, and the reason people get it wrong is that they answer it as though it were. There are four different events a value might have to live through, ordered here from cheap and frequent to rare and destructive, and they are not survived by the same mechanism. The second is the one most often skipped over, and it is the one that catches people out.

An owner that stays in the Composition, so hoisting the state to a caller that does not leave; or a `SaveableStateHolder` around the subtree, which is what navigation libraries use to give each destination its own saved state

Occasionally — a rotation, a theme change
A saved-state mechanism such as `rememberSaveable`, or an owner with a longer life such as a `ViewModel`
The process being killed by the system and recreated later with the user's task intact
Rarely, and never at a moment you control
A saved-state mechanism such as `rememberSaveable`, within the limits below; or durable storage. Not a `ViewModel` on its own

blocks.text: `remember` covers the first row and nothing beyond it. The documentation is explicit that while `remember` retains state across recompositions, the state is not retained across configuration changes — because the Composition is exactly what a configuration change discards.

The second row is worth separating out precisely because `rememberSaveable` does **not** answer it on its own. Both `remember` and `rememberSaveable` are tied to a position in the Composition, and when that position goes away the value goes with it — `rememberSaveable` deregisters itself from the saved-state registry as it leaves. Nothing has been saved, because no save was happening; the screen is simply still running. Keeping a value across that means either hoisting it to a caller that does not leave, or wrapping the subtree in a `SaveableStateHolder`, which snapshots the subtree's saveable state before disposing it and restores it when the same key is composed again. That is the machinery a navigation library uses to bring a screen's scroll position back when you press Back.

The third and fourth rows are where `rememberSaveable` earns its name. It behaves like `remember` in that it retains a value across recomposition, and additionally stores that value through the saved instance state mechanism, so it is restored across activity or process recreation. Using it is a one-word change at the call site.

What `rememberSaveable` is **not** is durable storage, and that distinction is the whole point of the lesson. It covers the fourth row — system-initiated process death with the user's task intact — because the value was written into a `Bundle` and handed back on recreation, and it covers it only within the limits that `Bundle` imposes. A database or a file is a different thing for a different job. Saved state is also not a guarantee against everything the user can do: it is not retained when the user themselves dismisses the activity, for instance by swiping it away from the recents screen, because at that point the user has said they are finished.

The saved-state guarantee described here is Android's, and it is documented precisely. This app also ships on desktop, iOS and web, where Compose Multiplatform documents lifecycle states and events but no equivalent statement about what a host restores. Treat `rememberSaveable` as participation in a host-provided saved-state mechanism whose Android behaviour is specified and whose behaviour elsewhere is not something to rely on. The part that holds everywhere — and the part an interview is asking about — is the ladder itself: re-execution, leaving the Composition, UI recreation, process recreation.
`rememberSaveable` stores UI element state in a `Bundle`, and it can put primitive types there automatically. Anything else needs to be told how to become storable, which is what a `Saver` is.

`listSaver` and `mapSaver` cover most cases; a type can also be made storable with the `Parcelize` annotation on Android, or a `Saver` can be implemented directly. When a type needs a `Saver` that is awkward to write, that is usually information rather than an obstacle: it is a hint that the object is bigger than the thing saved state is for.

Which brings up the size limit, which is the most common way this API is misused. The `Bundle` behind `rememberSaveable` is shared with everything else that writes to saved instance state, and its size is limited; storing large objects can produce a `TransactionTooLargeException` at runtime. This is particularly unpleasant in a single-activity app, where every screen contributes to the same `Bundle`, and it fails on real devices under memory pressure rather than on the developer's machine.

The guidance that follows from that is to store the minimum: identifiers and keys rather than the objects they identify, and then use those to restore the richer state from somewhere that is built to hold it.

The state that genuinely belongs here is small, transient, and a consequence of what the user has been doing rather than of what the app has loaded: a scroll position, whether a section is expanded, an in-progress selection, the text someone has typed but not submitted. Losing any of it is annoying rather than destructive, which is a useful test in both directions — if losing it would be destructive, saved state is the wrong mechanism.

Concluding that if `rememberSaveable` is stronger than `remember`, everything should use it. Every value that goes in competes for the same limited `Bundle`, needs to be storable, and costs work at exactly the moment the system is already under pressure. State that can be recomputed, refetched, or reasonably reset should not be saved at all.

The question that separates a memorised answer from an understood one is how `rememberSaveable`, a `ViewModel`, `SavedStateHandle` and durable storage relate to each other. They are frequently presented as competing options. They are not alternatives; they survive different things and are routinely used together.

blocks.text: The table deliberately leaves out the second row of the ladder, because the answer there is the same for both composable-scoped mechanisms and is not about the mechanism at all: neither `remember` nor `rememberSaveable` survives its own call site leaving the Composition. That is a question about where the state is owned, which is the next Lesson, or about wrapping the subtree in a `SaveableStateHolder`. A `ViewModel` scoped above the departing composable does survive it, which is one of the honest reasons to reach for one.

The row worth dwelling on is `ViewModel`. It handles configuration changes essentially for free, because the instance is kept across the activity being destroyed and recreated — but a `ViewModel` instance does not survive system-initiated process death. `SavedStateHandle` is what closes that gap, and it uses the same `Bundle` mechanism, which means it inherits the same advice: put simple UI element state in it, not screen state produced by business rules.

A realistic screen therefore uses several at once. The article list's scroll position is saved UI state; the identifier of the article being read is a small key in `SavedStateHandle`; the article itself is reloaded from the repository, which reads it from the database. Nothing here is a fallback for anything else. How screen-level state is owned and produced is the subject of the ViewModel unit later in this path; what this lesson fixes is the habit of asking "what does this have to survive?" before reaching for an API.

The reliable question is why `rememberSaveable` rather than `remember` for a text field that should survive rotation, and the reliable follow-up is whether you would save the whole object. Answer the first with the ladder — both retain across recomposition, only `rememberSaveable` participates in saved-state restoration — and the second with the `Bundle`: it is small, shared, and a `TransactionTooLargeException` is a real production failure, so save the id and reload the rest. If you can add that a `ViewModel` survives rotation but not process death, you have covered the ground most candidates miss.

lessons.title: State Hoisting and the Lowest Sensible Owner
lessons.summary: Moving state to a caller is mechanically trivial and the interesting part is entirely in the decision: who reads it, who writes it, and how long it must live. Including why hoisting too far is a real cost rather than a safe default.

blocks.text: A composable that owns state with `remember` is convenient and self-contained, and it stops being either as soon as anything else needs to know about that state. The parent cannot read it, a test cannot set it, a preview cannot show the interesting case, and a second component that ought to react to it has no way to find out. State hoisting is the move that fixes all of those at once: take the state out of the composable and give it to the caller, then pass the current value down and send events back up.

The result is a pair of terms worth using precisely. A **stateful** composable holds state of its own. A **stateless** composable holds none: everything it displays arrives as a parameter and everything the user does leaves as a callback. Hoisting converts the first into the second, and the second is what is reusable, previewable and testable.

That value-plus-callback shape is the same direction the previous unit established — state down, events up — applied to one component. This lesson is not about the direction, which is settled; it is about the question the direction raises and does not answer, which is how far up the state should go.
The documentation gives three rules, and they are unusually useful because they give a floor rather than a preference:

items: State should be hoisted to at least the lowest common parent of all composables that read it.
State should be hoisted to at least the highest level at which it may be changed.
If two pieces of state change in response to the same events, they should be hoisted together.

blocks.text: Each says "at least", so together they establish a minimum height, not a target. You may hoist higher than the rules require; the rules only tell you when you have not hoisted enough. Under-hoisting makes unidirectional data flow difficult or impossible to follow, because a value that has to be read above where it lives leaves you with no legal way to get at it.

Hoisting is not a quality gradient with "higher is better" at one end. The rules define the lowest position that works, and the useful instinct is to sit at that position rather than above it: keep state as close as possible to where it is consumed, and move it up only when something concrete requires the move.

The convention that makes hoisting cheap is the overload pair: a stateless implementation that does the work, and a stateful convenience overload that supplies default state for callers who do not care. Compose's own components are built this way, and it means hoisting later is not a breaking change.

Now consider the decision this lesson is really about. A settings screen has a switch. Where should `enabled` live? Work through the three tests. If only the switch reads it, the switch can own it. If a summary line elsewhere on the screen also shows it, the lowest common parent of the two is the screen, so it belongs there. If a save button has to submit it, the writer is higher again and it goes with whatever owns the form. And if it must survive a rotation, nothing moves at all: that is a question about the persistence mechanism, not about the owner, and the switch keeps the state with `rememberSaveable`.

The cost of getting this wrong in the upward direction is the one people underestimate, because over-hoisted code still works. Push every scrap of local UI state to the top of the screen and three things follow. The screen's state type accumulates fields that are nobody's business but one component's. Every component needs a parameter and a callback threaded down through the layers between, so adding a checkbox becomes an edit to four files. And a change to any one of those fields is now a change observed at the top of the tree, which widens the region of UI a single keystroke can affect — the reason the next unit treats read location as a design decision.

The step between a composable and a screen-level owner is a plain state holder class, and it is under-used. When several related pieces of state and the logic that coordinates them belong together, a normal Kotlin class remembered in the Composition keeps that logic testable without pulling it out of the UI layer.

Note the `private set` and the intent-named functions: the class is hoisted state with one write path, not a mutable bag. Because it lives in the Composition it follows the composable's lifecycle, which is what lets it hold Compose-owned types such as a `LazyListState`. What it must not hold is business logic or application data — that is where a screen-level owner takes over, and the `ViewModel` unit later in this path covers it.

Two collapses to avoid, and they are the same mistake in different clothes. Treating "hoist it" and "put it in the ViewModel" as the same instruction. They are different claims: hoisting says the state has an owner above this composable, and choosing a `ViewModel` says that owner must outlive the Composition and sits next to business logic. Whether a row is expanded is real state with a real owner, and that owner is almost never a `ViewModel`. And treating "it has to survive something" as a reason to hoist: where state lives and how long it persists are chosen separately, which is why a composable can own its state and still keep it across a rotation.

The framing that survives contact with a real codebase is not "Compose state or `ViewModel` state" but a single question asked of each piece of state: who is its lowest sensible owner? Three tests answer it, and they are worth running explicitly rather than by feel.

items: Who reads it? The owner must be at or above the lowest common ancestor of every reader.
Who writes it? The owner must be at or above everything that can change it, including a save button, a retry, or a navigation event.

How long must it live? This is the test that is most often misread, because lifetime and ownership are separate axes. Surviving the UI being recreated is a mechanism question that `rememberSaveable` answers without the state moving anywhere. Ownership only has to change when the state must outlive the composable's own place in the Composition — a branch that closes, a screen popped off a back stack — and surviving the process needs saved or durable storage whoever owns it.

blocks.text: The third test is what makes the lowest common ancestor sometimes lie outside the Composition entirely, which the documentation states directly: the ancestor may be a `ViewModel` when business logic is involved. That is not an exception to the rule, it is the rule producing an owner that happens not to be a composable.

A distinction from the architecture guidance sharpens this further. **UI element state** is intrinsic to how an element renders — expanded or collapsed, scrolled here, focused. **Screen UI state** is what the screen has to show, produced by applying business rules to application data. Screen UI state is hoisted to a screen-level owner essentially by definition, because that is where business rules are. UI element state stays local unless something drags it upward — and the thing that usually does is business logic needing to read or write it, at which point it stops being purely intrinsic.

Two more consequences worth being able to state. First, ownership is what makes unidirectional data flow enforceable rather than aspirational: one owner per piece of state means every change has exactly one code path, which is the property that makes a wrong screen debuggable. Second, hoisting is reversible and cheap to revisit when the overload-pair convention is used, so the right instinct is to start at the lowest position the three rules allow and move up when a concrete requirement — not a hypothetical one — appears.

Expect "what is state hoisting and why?" and answer with the ownership decision rather than the mechanics, which take one sentence. Say that hoisting moves state to an appropriate owner — at least the lowest common ancestor of everything that reads it and at least as high as anything that writes it — and passes the value down with events coming up, which makes the child stateless, reusable and testable. Then pre-empt the follow-up: hoisting is not the same as moving state into a `ViewModel`, and hoisting further than required costs you parameter threading, a bloated screen state type, and a wider region of UI affected by every small change.

lessons.title: Collections and Observable Mutation
lessons.summary: Adding to a list held in state is the most reliable way to produce a screen that silently refuses to update. Why the mutation is invisible, the three ways to fix it, and why a `List` parameter guarantees you less than it appears to.

blocks.text: Everything so far has quietly assumed that the value in a state holder is replaced when it changes. For an `Int` or a `String` that assumption is free, because there is no other way to change them. For a collection there is another way, it is the way everyone reaches for first, and it does not work.

The list really does grow. Log its size and it climbs with every click. The screen shows nothing new, and the reason is visible once you look at what was written: `add` mutates the object that `value` refers to. It never assigns to `value`. The state holder is the observable thing, and from its point of view nothing has happened — it is still pointing at the same list it was pointing at before.

Compose observes the state holder, not arbitrary objects. `MutableState` reports a change when its `value` is written; it has no way to learn that something inside the object it holds was modified. Mutable objects that are not themselves observable — an `ArrayList`, a `mutableListOf`, a data class with `var` properties — do not trigger recomposition when they change.

So the fix is to write to `value`, which in practice means producing a new list rather than editing the existing one. The documented recommendation is exactly this: instead of non-observable mutable objects, use an observable holder such as `State<List<T>>` together with the read-only `listOf()`.

Two things changed and both matter. The declared type is now `List<String>` rather than `MutableList<String>`, so the mutating methods are not even reachable through this reference, and the operation is an assignment rather than an in-place edit, so the holder sees a write. Choosing the read-only type is not cosmetic here — it removes the shape of the bug from the code.
Replacement covers most cases, and Kotlin's collection operators make it read well enough that it rarely feels like a workaround.

The alternative is a collection that is itself observable. `mutableStateListOf` and `mutableStateMapOf` produce snapshot-aware collections where the mutating operations are the notification, so `add` and `remove` work the way the broken example expected them to.

blocks.text: The default should be the left-hand column. `mutableStateListOf` earns its place when a list is large, edited often and owned locally; reaching for it because in-place mutation feels more natural is how Compose runtime types end up in a data layer that should not know Compose exists.
The same invisibility appears one level down, and it is harder to spot because the outer assignment looks correct.

The second line is the instructive one, because it looks like the fix. A generated `copy()` is shallow — constructor property values are passed to a new instance — so both objects reference the same `MutableList`. Mutating it changes the old instance too, the two compare equal, and `mutableStateOf` treats an assignment of an equal value as no change. The real fix is to make the nested data immutable as well, so that changing it produces a genuinely different value.

blocks.code:
data class Filters(val tags: List<String> = emptyList())

filters = filters.copy(tags = filters.tags + "kotlin")

blocks.text: Diagnosing this as a recomposition problem and going looking for what to optimise. The composable is not failing to recompose for a subtle reason; nothing asked it to. Before investigating anything else, check whether a write to a state holder actually happened — for a collection or a nested object, usually it did not.

There is a Kotlin fact underneath all of this that is worth stating exactly, because the loose version of it causes its own bugs. `List` is a read-only interface, not an immutable type. Declaring a parameter as `List<String>` removes the mutating methods from that reference and guarantees nothing whatsoever about the underlying object, which may still be held as a `MutableList` somewhere else and changed while you are looking at it. No copy is made by the conversion.

A composable given `repository.items` holds a reference that can change contents without any assignment happening anywhere it can see. Nothing is observable, nothing is scheduled, and the screen is wrong in a way that no amount of reading the composable will explain. If a caller needs a value that cannot change under it, it has to copy explicitly or the producer has to hand over a genuinely immutable collection.

This is also the doorway into the next major idea in the Compose path. Because collection types carry that guarantee gap, Compose cannot assume that a `List` parameter which compares equal actually means unchanged — collections such as `List`, `Set` and `Map` are treated as unstable for precisely this reason. What stability is, what the runtime does with it, and how it decides whether work can be skipped are the subject of the identity and stability unit; the piece to carry forward from here is that read-only is a property of a reference, and immutability is a property of an object, and Compose cares about the second.

"I add to a list in state and the UI does not update — why?" is a standard debugging question and the answer is one sentence: the mutation never wrote to the state holder, and Compose observes the holder rather than the object inside it. Have both fixes ready — replace the list, or use a snapshot-aware collection — and a reason to prefer replacement at layer boundaries. The stronger follow-up material is that `copy()` is shallow and that a read-only `List` is not an immutable one, which is where the same bug hides after the obvious version has been fixed.

units.title: Recomposition
units.summary: Recomposition is the mechanism that turns a state change into a different screen, and it is routinely described in a way that makes it sound both more dramatic and less predictable than it is. This unit separates the steps — a write, an invalidation, an execution, a frame — shows how the location of a state read decides how much work a change can cause, and ends by disposing of the belief that recomposition is itself a performance defect. The units on stability and derived state are answers to problems framed here.

lessons.title: Composition and Recomposition
lessons.summary: What actually happens between a button being clicked and the screen looking different: a write, an invalidation, a scheduled execution, and a frame — four separate things that a single sentence about recomposition usually collapses into one.

blocks.text: Two units have now supplied the halves of the mechanism. The first said that a composable contributes a description of UI to the Composition and that the runtime may run that description again. The second said that reading a state value during execution records a dependency, and writing it schedules recomposition of whatever recorded one. This lesson puts them together and, more usefully, takes apart the single word that hides the details.

Start with the two events in the title. **Initial composition** is the first run: the composables you called are executed, and the Composition — the runtime's record of what your UI currently is — is built from what they emitted. **Recomposition** is a later re-execution of part of that work, in response to state that was read having changed, which updates the existing Composition rather than rebuilding it from nothing. A composable's whole lifecycle is exactly this: it enters the Composition, is recomposed zero or more times, and leaves.
"Zero or more" is worth pausing on. A composable that is displayed for a minute and never recomposed is not idle or broken; it simply read nothing that changed. Recomposition is not a heartbeat.

Recomposition is Compose re-executing the composables that may have changed in response to state changes, and then updating the Composition to reflect any changes. Every word of that is load-bearing: it re-executes some composables, not all of them; it does so because state changed, not on a timer; and what it updates is the description, which is not yet the screen.
That last clause is where most confusion lives, so it is worth naming the three phases now rather than later. Producing a frame runs through them in order, and composition is only the first.

rows: Composition
*What* to show
Runs composable functions and produces a description of the UI.
Layout
*Where* to put it
Measures each element and places it, in two steps, in 2D coordinates.
Drawing
*How* it renders
Draws the elements into a canvas — usually the device screen.

blocks.text: Recomposition is a re-run of the first phase only. Whether the other two follow is a separate question with a real answer: conceptually each phase happens for every frame, but Compose avoids repeating work that would compute the same result from the same inputs, and it may skip layout and drawing entirely when the content, size and position are unchanged. So "recomposition redraws the screen" is not a simplification, it is wrong in both directions — a recomposition need not reach drawing, and drawing can happen with no recomposition at all when the state that changed was read during the draw phase.

Describing recomposition as rebuilding the layout tree and remeasuring and redrawing it on every state change. That describes neither what recomposition is nor what it triggers. Recomposition re-executes the affected composables and applies the difference to the Composition; measuring and drawing are later phases that Compose runs only to the extent the change actually requires.
Take a concrete interaction and follow it the whole way. A screen with a counter and a static header, plus a click.

Before the click, initial composition has already run: `CounterScreen`, `Header`, `CountLabel` and the `Button` all executed once, the Composition holds what they emitted, and the remembered state holder sits in `CounterScreen`'s slot. Note which code read `count`. The body of `CounterScreen` did, in order to pass it as an argument. `CountLabel` did not — it read its `count` parameter, which is an ordinary `Int`, not the state object.
Now the user taps the button. Four distinct things happen, in this order.

items: **An event.** The `onClick` lambda runs. This is ordinary code running once, because a click happened — it is not composition, and nothing is being described.
**A write to observable state.** `count++` reads the current value and assigns a new one. Because the new value differs from the old under the default equality policy, this counts as a change.

**Invalidation.** The runtime marks the regions that recorded a read of that state object as out of date and schedules them. Here that is the body of `CounterScreen`. Nothing has executed yet; being invalid is a recorded fact, not an action.

**Execution and application.** On the next composition pass the runtime runs the invalidated code, `CounterScreen`'s body produces a description with `count` = 1, the difference is applied to the Composition, and the layout and drawing phases then do whatever that difference requires.

blocks.text: Which composables re-executed? `CounterScreen`'s body did, and `CountLabel` did because it was called with a different argument. `Header` did not: it is called with the same `String` it had before, so the runtime can skip it. The button's content lambda emits a constant `Text` and has no reason to produce anything new either. One state change, one label updated — not a screen rebuilt.

Keeping steps three and four apart is what makes the rest of this unit predictable. Invalidation is bookkeeping and is nearly free; execution is the thing that costs something and happens later, on the runtime's schedule. Several writes in quick succession do not queue up several executions of the same code — the scope is already invalid, and one pass brings it up to date with the newest values. This is why counting assignments tells you nothing about how many times a composable ran, and why neither number is the number of frames drawn.

The order above is causal, not temporal in any guaranteed way. A state write does not synchronously call your composable, so code after `count++` in the same lambda cannot assume the UI has caught up, and there is no supported way to ask "has it recomposed yet?". Write the next state instead of waiting for the last one.
This is also the concrete reason the previous unit's rule about side effects is a contract rather than advice. Consider a line placed in `CountLabel`.

What does the resulting number mean? Not how many times the user saw a count, because `CountLabel` may be skipped when the value is unchanged, may run because something unrelated in its parent was invalidated, and may run as part of work that is later discarded. The count is a property of the runtime's scheduling decisions. Neither the number of executions nor their order relative to sibling composables is something the API promises, so nothing whose correctness depends on either belongs in a composable body. Work caused by a user action belongs in the event callback, where the click really did happen once; work that genuinely belongs to the composition itself belongs to Compose's effect APIs, which give it a defined lifetime, and which have their own unit later in this path.
Two refinements separate a confident answer from a recited one, and both are about not over-promising.

The first is that recomposition is optimistic. Compose expects to finish a recomposition before the parameters change again, and if they do change first it may cancel that recomposition and restart it with the new values. Work performed during an execution that gets cancelled is thrown away — which is fine for a description and not at all fine for anything that had an effect elsewhere. This is the same argument as the side-effect rule, arriving from a different direction: the runtime reserves the right to discard an execution, which is only sound if executing had no consequences beyond the description.

The second is about frequency. Composable functions may be re-executed as often as every frame, for instance while an animation is running. That is not a pathology to be designed away; it is the normal operating mode of a framework whose job is to describe the current state cheaply. It does, however, mean the body is on a path that can run sixty times a second, which is what makes "fast" part of the contract alongside idempotent and side-effect free.

It is worth being precise about what the phases buy, without straying into performance work that belongs later. Because the three phases are separate and each tracks its own state reads, a change can enter the pipeline at different points: state read during composition schedules a re-run of composition, state read during layout schedules layout, and state read only during drawing schedules just the draw phase. Even the measurement and placement steps within layout have separate restart scopes. That is the mechanism behind a fact worth carrying into the next lesson — the screen can change without anything recomposing — and the technique that exploits it deliberately belongs to the performance unit.

"How does initial composition differ from recomposition?" is a standard opener. Say that initial composition executes the composables once to build the Composition and record what UI to emit, and that recomposition re-executes only the parts whose observed state changed and applies the difference, skipping composables whose inputs are unchanged. Then add the sentence most answers omit: composition is separate from layout and drawing, so recomposition does not remeasure and redraw the screen, and state read only during layout or drawing can change what is displayed without recomposing anything at all.

lessons.title: Recomposition Scopes and Selective Execution
lessons.summary: The same state, read in two different places, invalidates two different amounts of your screen. What a recomposition scope actually is, why extracting a function is not the same as creating one, and why the read location rather than the write location decides the blast radius.

blocks.text: The previous lesson said the runtime invalidates "the regions that recorded a read". That phrase was doing a lot of work, and this lesson unpacks it, because the size of those regions is the difference between a keystroke updating one label and a keystroke re-executing an entire screen.

A **recomposition scope** is a region of code the runtime can re-run on its own. The compiler generates that capability for composable functions by default — the annotation that opts out of it, `@NonRestartableComposable`, exists precisely to prevent code being generated that allows a function's execution to be skipped or restarted. When state is read, the subscription is recorded against the scope that is executing at that moment. The runtime's own description of `MutableState` says it exactly: reads to `value` during the execution of a composable subscribe the currently executing recompose scope, and a write schedules recomposition of the scopes so subscribed.

The read is recorded by whoever is running, not by whoever declared the state and not by whoever wrote to it. Two composables reading the same state object have two independent subscriptions; a composable that never reads it has none, however close to the state it sits in the source.
So compare two versions of the same screen. They render identically and differ only in where the state is read.

In version A the read happens in `ProfileScreenA`'s own body, because producing the argument `name = name` requires reading `value` there. That body is therefore the subscribed scope, and typing a character invalidates the whole of it. In version B `ProfileScreenB` passes the holder without reading it; the read happens inside `NameField`, so `NameField` is the subscribed scope and typing invalidates only that.
Note what did **not** change: the state lives in the same place in both versions, and it is written from the same place. Only the read moved, and that alone moved the invalidation.

Version A is not a bug, and this is the point at which people usually overcorrect. Invalidating a scope means the runtime will re-run it; it does not mean everything inside it does expensive work again. When `ProfileScreenA`'s body re-executes it calls `ExpensiveChart` with the same `data` argument, and a composable whose inputs are unchanged can be skipped rather than run. In a well-behaved tree the practical difference between A and B is often small.

It stops being small when skipping cannot happen, and the honest summary at this stage of the path is that whether a given call is skipped depends on the types of its arguments and on how the compiler is configured — which is the subject of the next unit, not something to guess at here. What version B gives you is independence from that question: work that is never invalidated does not need to be skippable.

Two separate things are easy to merge into one. **Invalidation** is what a state write does to the scopes that read that state. **Skipping** is a decision the runtime makes about a call it reaches while executing an invalidated scope. Narrowing the read narrows invalidation; stability decides skipping. This lesson is about the first.

Now the trap. Having seen that moving a read into `NameField` narrowed things, it is natural to conclude that wrapping code in something — anything — creates a boundary. It does not, and the counter-example is the most common construct in Compose.

`Column`, `Row` and `Box` are declared `inline`, so their content lambdas are compiled into the calling function rather than existing as separate functions the runtime could restart. The read of `name` inside that inner `Column` is a read inside `ProfileScreenC`, and the whole body is invalidated exactly as it would be without the wrapper. Nesting layout does not partition anything.

The same caution applies to extracting a helper: it is the *kind* of function that matters, not the act of extraction. A composable function that returns `Unit` and is not inline gives you a scope. A function that is inline does not. A composable with a non-`Unit` return type is not eligible for skipping either, which is one reason the convention is that composables emit UI rather than return it.
