blocks.text: The middle column is where the misconception lives. `derivedStateOf` does not memoize the calculation away: once a dependency has changed, the calculation runs again the next time the value is consulted. What the measurement below removed was executions of the reader, not of the calculation.

Measured on this project's JVM target: a composable scope read a derived `showButton` while an index was driven 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4, letting the runtime settle after each write. The derived calculation ran five times — the initial composition plus one per settled change. The scope reading it executed twice: once initially, and once when the Boolean flipped at 0 → 1. The three later index changes invalidated nobody. That count belongs to this schedule rather than to the API, for a reason the deeper section takes up.
Now the case where it earns nothing, which is far more common in real code than the case where it earns something.

The guide calls this out by name: a common mistake is to assume that combining two Compose state objects means you are "deriving state" and therefore want `derivedStateOf`, and it describes the result as purely overhead. The reasoning transfers well past the example, and it is worth stating in the general form — the number of inputs is not the test. Two values combined into a result that changes whenever either of them changes leave no frequency mismatch to exploit, so the filter has nothing to filter.

The same measurement run against a trivial derived expression — a label rebuilt from an index that changed at every step — shows precisely that. The consumer executed five times with the wrapper and five times without it, and the wrapper added a derived-state object, its dependency bookkeeping, and a comparison on every change. The documentation's caution is blunt about the trade: `derivedStateOf` is expensive, and it should only be used to avoid unnecessary recomposition when a result has not changed.

Three promises `derivedStateOf` does not make. It does not memoize the calculation away — a changed dependency means the calculation runs again the next time the value is needed. It does not eliminate recomposition — the reader still executes whenever the result genuinely differs, and every other scope on the screen is untouched either way. And it does not make an expensive computation affordable: a costly calculation inside a derived state is paid for again on every dependency change that gets observed, while you *hope* the result repeats. An expensive calculation behind a fast-changing input is a memoization or a placement problem, and this is neither tool.

The rule that transfers to a problem you have not seen before is a short interrogation, and it does not mention an API until the end. Name the inputs. Name the result the consumer actually observes. Estimate how often each of them changes. If they change at roughly the same rate, calculate directly. If the inputs are expensive to process and change less often than the body executes, that is `remember` with keys. Only when a cheap-to-evaluate result changes much less often than its inputs is there anything for `derivedStateOf` to remove.
`derivedStateOf` creates an object, and everything surprising about it follows from that.

First, it needs a `remember`. Written bare in a composable body it constructs a new derived state on every execution, discarding the recorded dependencies and the cached result the whole mechanism depends on — all of the cost and none of the benefit. `remember { derivedStateOf { ... } }` is the shape for a reason, not as idiom.

Second, the object lives as long as its `remember` does — the presence of that call site in the Composition — and its calculation captures **everything** that was in scope when it was created. That capture is where correctness goes wrong, because a captured ordinary value is frozen at creation while a captured `State` is read afresh on every recalculation. Note the word *everything*: the trap is not one input, it is every non-`State` value the lambda closes over.

Measured on this project's JVM target: with the threshold changed from 1 to 5 and the index then moved to 2, the flag reported `true`. Two is not past five — the derived state was still comparing against the 1 it had captured. The fix is to key the `remember` on every captured value, `remember(listState, threshold)`, or to make those inputs snapshot state so the calculation reads them instead of closing over them. Keying on `threshold` alone would look like a fix and would not be one: `listState` is captured on exactly the same terms, so a caller that supplies a different `LazyListState` would keep a derived value still watching the previous list's scroll position. That is the under-specified key of the first lesson in this unit, arriving in a place where it is much harder to see.

Third, the calculation is pulled rather than pushed, and this is the part that corrects the cost model. A write to a dependency marks the derived value invalid; nothing is recalculated until that value is next read, or until the runtime checks whether a scope that read it has to be invalidated. Two measurements on this project's JVM target make the difference concrete. Four writes with no opportunity for the runtime to settle between them produced **one** recalculation rather than four. A derived state that was created and remembered but whose value was never read ran its calculation **zero** times, across the initial composition and four subsequent writes to its dependency.

So "the calculation runs on every dependency change" is a useful first approximation and not a rule. The honest version is that a dependency change invalidates the value and the calculation re-runs the next time somebody needs it, which means an execution count for a derived state describes the observation schedule as much as it describes the code. The practical advice is unchanged and now rests on something true: what `derivedStateOf` saves is consumer invalidation, and it is not the tool for making an expensive calculation cheap.

One point of mechanism is worth having, and only one. The runtime this project resolves offers two overloads — `derivedStateOf(calculation)` and `derivedStateOf(policy, calculation)` — where the policy decides what counts as a changed result. Its documentation notes that a derived state carrying no policy signals an update on every dependency change and leaves it to the observer to decide whether that matters, and Compose's own recomposition machinery is exactly such an observer: before invalidating a scope that read a derived value it compares the new result against the one that scope last saw, using structural equality when no policy was supplied. That is why the plain overload behaves inside a composable the way the guide describes. It also means the filter is only as good as the result type's `equals` — a derived state returning a freshly built object that no two runs consider equal filters nothing at all. How the snapshot system records and compares these reads is the next unit's subject; this is as far into it as the decision needs to go.

Expect the scroll-to-top question, and expect it to be a trap for anyone who learned the example rather than the rule. Lead with the frequency mismatch — the index changes with every scrolled row, the Boolean changes twice — and say precisely what is saved: readers of the derived value are not invalidated while the result is unchanged. Then give the counter-case unprompted, because it is what separates understanding from recall — combining two state values into a result that changes as often as they do is not a use for `derivedStateOf`, it is overhead. If you can add that the calculation itself is not saved — a changed dependency invalidates the value and the calculation re-runs when it is next needed — you have described the API rather than repeated the slogan.

lessons.title: Keeping Work Out of Composition
lessons.summary: Memoization answers "how often does this run". It never answers "whose job is this". Where the line falls between a calculation that can stay in a composable, one that needs an owner above the UI, and an operation that must not appear in a composable body at all — and why moving code to a ViewModel is not the same as moving it off the main thread.

blocks.text: Every tool in this unit so far has left the work where it was and changed how often it happens. That is the right move for one class of problem and the wrong move for another, and the two are separated by a question none of the previous lessons asked: whose responsibility is this in the first place?

A composable body describes UI. The runtime executes it, potentially as often as every frame, in an order you do not control, and it may abandon an execution before it finishes — Unit 1's execution contract, unchanged. Nothing in that description makes it a good host for work whose correctness depends on running once, in order, or at a particular moment.
Three bands settle most decisions, and the middle one is the only one that takes real thought.

rows: Formatting a label, choosing a colour, picking which of two branches to emit
In the composable, calculated directly
It is presentation, it is cheap, and it exists only for this screen. Extracting it buys nothing and costs indirection
Filtering, sorting, grouping or mapping a substantial collection into what the screen shows
A deliberate decision: memoized here if it is genuinely this screen's presentation, owned above the UI if it is the screen's state
The result is identical on most executions, so repeating it is waste — but the more telling question is whether this describes the data or decides what it means
Reading a file, calling a repository, writing to a database, applying a business rule
Never in a composable body

Composition has nowhere to put a result, no cancellation of its own, and no guarantee about how often or whether an execution completes. Business logic belongs in the domain or data layers and never in the UI layer

blocks.text: The guide that introduces `remember` for expensive calculations attaches a note to it that is easy to skim past and is this lesson's entire point: if possible, it is best to move calculations outside of the composable altogether — sorting the list elsewhere, such as in the `ViewModel`, and passing the sorted list in as an input.

`remember` makes repeated work happen once. It does not make misplaced work correctly placed. "How expensive is this?" and "whose job is this?" are separate questions, and the second one has answers the first cannot reach.
Held against the middle band, code that looks the same splits along a line that has very little to do with cost.

Neither choice is about how long the operation takes. The row's label would still belong in the row if it were slightly expensive, and the order filter would still belong above the UI if it were trivially cheap, because a second consumer already needs the same answer.
The bottom band deserves to be explicit, because the failure it produces is not a slow screen but a wrong one.

The `remember` is doing real work here — the call happens once per `userId` instead of on every execution — and the code is still wrong. A blocking read now sits on the thread running composition; the call cannot be cancelled when the screen goes away; there is no loading or error state, because a composable body has nowhere to express one; and if the composable leaves the Composition and is re-entered, the work starts again from nothing. Memoization made the symptom rarer and left every one of those properties exactly as it found them.

Using `remember` as a substitute for placement — "I wrapped the call in `remember`, so it only runs once." Running once was not the property that was missing. What was missing is an owner that outlives the screen, can report loading and failure, and can be cancelled; and no cache placed **inside** the thing that is supposed to be cancelled can supply any of it.

There is a second separation to make, and getting it wrong is the most common way a fix fails to fix anything. **Moving work to a `ViewModel` or a use case moves the responsibility. It does not move the thread.** A function called from a `ViewModel` runs on whatever thread called it, and that is very often the main thread. Kotlin's guidance puts the duty with the code doing the work rather than with its caller: a class performing long-running blocking operations is in charge of moving execution off the main thread, and that applies to every class in the app regardless of which part of the architecture it sits in. Memoization is not background execution either — `remember` runs its lambda synchronously, during composition, on composition's thread.

Which coroutine builder, which dispatcher, and which effect API carries suspending work into a composable are real questions with careful answers, and they belong to the effects and coroutine material later in this path. What this lesson needs from them is only the boundary: "somewhere else" and "some other thread" are two decisions, and making one does not make the other.

The layering argument is short, and it stops early on purpose. The UI layer's job is to consume application data, convert it into something the UI can present, and display it; the state holder — usually a `ViewModel` at screen level — is the class responsible for producing that state and for the logic that produces it; business logic is placed in the domain or data layers and never in the UI layer. That is enough to answer "not in the composable". It is deliberately not enough to answer "therefore write a use case".

The domain layer is documented as optional. The guidance says plainly that not every app needs one, that use cases should be added only when required — for complex business logic, or simple logic reused by several state holders — and that the cost of ignoring this is being forced to add use cases that are simple pass-through calls to the data layer, complexity for little benefit. So "move it out of the composable" does not resolve to a fixed destination. Four questions decide it, and they are worth asking in this order.

items: **Cost.** How expensive is one execution, and is it on a path that runs often? A cheap calculation on a screen that rarely recomposes has no problem to solve.
**Lifetime.** How long must the result outlive whatever produced it? Anything that has to survive longer than a composable's presence in the Composition cannot be owned by a composable.
**Reuse.** Does anything else need the same answer? A second consumer is the clearest signal that a calculation is not presentation.
**Responsibility.** Does this describe the data or decide what it means? Decisions about meaning are business logic, and that is the one band with no discretion.

blocks.text: None of that is a measurement, and saying so matters. The costs described throughout this unit are engineering reasoning about where work sits and how often it repeats — illustrative, not benchmarked — and nothing here claims how many milliseconds any of it takes. Unit 3's standard for turning an observation into a finding is unchanged and applies to placement too: a symptom someone could notice, expensive work identified on the path that produces it, and a causal link between the two. Restructuring code because a diagram says it belongs elsewhere, with no symptom and no measurement, is the same mistake as chasing a recomposition count.

The mirror-image error deserves an equally clear warning, because this lesson is the one most likely to cause it. "All calculations must leave composition" is not the conclusion. A screen that formats two fields and picks a colour from a status has nothing to move, and moving it produces a state holder that exists to perform string concatenation. The genuinely interesting cases feel obvious in hindsight because they fail several of the four questions at once: expensive, needed beyond this screen, wanted by more than one consumer, and a decision about data rather than a description of it.

The question arrives as "how do you handle an expensive operation in a composable?", and the checklist answer — `remember`, `derivedStateOf`, stability — is the weak one, because it never asks what the operation is. Split it instead: cheap presentation stays and is calculated directly; a repeated pure transformation is memoized against its inputs; anything that reads, writes or decides belongs above the UI and arrives at the screen as state. Then add the sentence most candidates miss — moving it to a `ViewModel` changes who owns it, not which thread it runs on, and main-safety is the responsibility of the code doing the work.

units.title: Snapshot Fundamentals
units.summary: Four units have each answered a different question, and every answer rested on the same unstated machinery: something has to notice that a value changed and work out who cared. This unit names that machinery and stops there. One model — state objects that report reads and changes, contexts that record reads while they run, and invalidation that marks whoever recorded one — explains why the counter did not count, why the list did not appear, why moving a read moved the blast radius, and why a derived value can decline to wake its reader. The second lesson takes the same model somewhere the UI is not, turning observable state into a `Flow` a coroutine can process.

lessons.title: How Compose Observes State
lessons.summary: The last four units each ended with a rule. All of them come from one mechanism: state objects that report reads and changes, a context that is recording reads while it runs, and invalidation that marks whoever recorded one as out of date. What that model promises, what it does not, and how to use it to find the cause of an update that never arrived.

blocks.text: Each of the last four units left you holding a rule. A plain `var` changes and the screen does not. Adding to a list held in state updates nothing. Moving a read into a child narrows how much re-executes. A derived value can decline to wake the composable reading it. Those read like four separate facts about four separate APIs. They are one mechanism seen from four angles, and this lesson names it.

The mechanism is the **snapshot system**, and the first thing to understand about it is that Compose's state objects are not ordinary containers. The values produced by `mutableStateOf`, `mutableStateListOf`, `mutableStateMapOf` and `derivedStateOf` report what happens to them. When one of them is read, whatever is currently recording reads is told which object was read. When one of them is changed, everything that recorded a read of it is marked out of date.
Four things therefore have to line up before anything appears on screen.

items: **An observable state object.** Only Compose's own state types take part. An `Int` field, an `ArrayList`, a `var` on a class you wrote — none of them can report anything, so none of them is inside this mechanism at all.

**A read that happens inside an observing context.** An observing context is code that is recording reads while it runs: a composable executing during composition, a `derivedStateOf` calculation, and — as the next lesson shows — a `snapshotFlow` block. Reading the same object from a click handler, or from an ordinary function running outside any observing context, returns the current value and records no dependency. An ordinary helper called during composition does participate in the caller's observing context, as Unit 3 explained.

**A change the state object agrees is a change.** `mutableStateOf` compares the new value against the current one with structural equality by default, so assigning a value equal to the one already held is not a change and is never reported.
**Invalidation.** What a reported change actually does is mark the contexts that recorded a read as out of date. It does not run them, and it certainly does not draw anything.

blocks.text: That last point is the one worth slowing down on, because the word people reach for is "refresh" and nothing about a write refreshes anything. A write is a recording, not a command. It leaves behind the information that some set of contexts is now describing an old value, and the runtime decides when to act on that — possibly coalescing several changes that arrive together into one pass. Composition is also only the first of three phases, with layout and drawing after it, so "the screen has caught up" is a strictly later event than "a write happened".

Observation is a relationship between a state object and a read, established at the moment of the read, by whichever context was recording at the time. Declaring state, passing it as a parameter, and writing to it all create nothing. This is why "why didn't my UI update?" almost always resolves into one of two findings: no observable change was reported, or the read that would have recorded the dependency happened somewhere other than where you assumed.

Two assumptions are worth stating plainly, because the model is easy to over-generalise in both directions. Not every read subscribes anything: a read outside an observing context is just a read. And not every write produces an update: a write of an equal value is not a change, and a genuine change that no context ever read invalidates nobody.

The quickest way to make the model usable is to take three screens that fail in exactly the same visible way — a value demonstrably changes and the UI does not move — and find a different cause in each.

`Cart` is an ordinary class. Its field can be read inside a composable perfectly well, and that read is recorded against nothing, because there is nothing in an ordinary field to do the reporting. Measured on this project's JVM target: after the field was changed from 0 to 1, the composable did not execute again, and reading the field afterwards confirmed it really did hold 1. No part of the mechanism was ever involved.

This one is more interesting, because a state object *is* present and the composable *is* reading it — `items.value` is a genuine recorded read. Measured on the same target: after `add`, the list held two elements and the composable still did not execute again. The dependency was recorded on the holder, and the holder was never written. `add` changed the object the holder points at, which the holder has no way to notice. This is the failure Unit 2's lesson on collections and observable mutation exists for, and its three fixes live there.

State object, recorded read, and a write that reaches the holder — and still nothing. Measured: assigning 0 to a state already holding 0 produced no execution at all, while the assignment of 1 that followed produced one. The default policy compares with structural equality, an equal value is not a change, and there was consequently nothing to report.

blocks.text: Those four rows diagnose those four examples, and that is exactly the limit of what this lesson claims. "Nothing observable was written" is the first thing to check and it is not a universal explanation for stale UI. A composable can lose its state because its identity changed rather than because a write was missed. A `remember` can hand back a stale result because a captured value was never made a key. A change can be reported correctly and the consumer still be skipped because its parameters compared equal. Those are the identity, stability and derived-state units' subjects, and they are separate failures with separate fixes. What this model gives you is the question that tells them apart: was a change reported at all? If it was, the problem is downstream of observation and this is not the lesson you need.

Reading "invalidated" as "executed". An invalidated scope is scheduled, not run, and how many times it eventually runs is not something to reason about: changes that land together can be coalesced into a single pass, and a call whose inputs did not change can be skipped inside that pass. Reason about which contexts a change *can* invalidate, which is well defined, and stop there.

Derived state is not an exception to any of this, and noticing that is what makes the model feel like one idea rather than a list. `derivedStateOf` produces a state object, so reading its value inside a composable records a dependency exactly as reading a `mutableStateOf` does. Its calculation is itself an observing context, which is why the state the calculation reads is what the derived value depends on — and why a value the calculation merely closed over is not. And the reason a derived value can withhold an update is the third item in the list above: before invalidating a context that read the result, the runtime compares the new result against the one that context last saw, and an equal result is not a change. One mechanism, applied at two levels.

The name is worth unpacking, because "snapshot" is not decoration. A snapshot is a view of the values of state objects, and the guarantee the runtime documents for it is narrow and precise: every state object has the same value inside the snapshot that it had when the snapshot was taken, unless it is explicitly changed inside that snapshot. Code reading state inside one is therefore pinned to a single version of the world — a write landing elsewhere while it reads does not change what it sees partway through.

Be careful how far you carry that, because it is the sentence most likely to be over-claimed in an interview. The guarantee is about state objects — the values held by `mutableStateOf`, the snapshot-aware collections, and derived state. It does not make your own classes transactional, it does not make an `ArrayList` safe to share between threads, and it does not turn an ordinary object graph into anything it was not before. An object reached *through* a state object is still just an object; only the holder takes part. That is the same boundary as the collection failure above, seen from the other side.

What consistency buys, and the reason it belongs in a lesson about observation at all, is that reading Compose state from somewhere that is not composition is a reasonable thing to do: a reader is never handed a value that shifts underneath it mid-read. The next lesson is built directly on that property.

There is a second limit, and it is the one that actually bites in production code. The guarantee is about one version of the values; it is not a guarantee about one *update* of yours. Two ordinary assignments to two state holders are two separate changes, and an observer that gets a chance to run between them sees the first holder's new value beside the second holder's old one. Measured on this project's JVM target: a reader of both holders observed the pair `(1, 0)` between `(0, 0)` and `(1, 1)` when each write was applied before the next was made, and observed only `(0, 0)` and `(1, 1)` when both writes landed before either was applied. The second outcome is a scheduling accident rather than a promise, so it is not something to design around. When two values form one invariant, the answer is not to hope they are written closely enough together — it is to put them in one state object, so that changing them is a single assignment of a single new value. That is the conclusion Unit 2 reached about collections and nested data, arriving here from the other direction.

The design question worth being able to answer is why the system records reads at all, when the write is the thing that actually happens. The answer is that a write knows nothing useful. A state object has no idea which parts of a UI display it; only the act of reading, performed by code that was recording at the time, establishes that relationship. Recording reads is therefore the only way to get invalidation proportional to what is genuinely affected instead of proportional to the size of the tree. It is also why the same machinery extends past composition: anything that can record reads can be a dependent, whether that is a composable, a derived calculation, the layout and drawing phases that track their own reads, or a coroutine building a stream.

Expect "how does Compose know when to recompose?" and answer it as a mechanism rather than an API list. State objects report reads and writes; a read performed while an observing context is running records that context as a dependent; a change — a write the state object's own policy agrees is a change — invalidates the contexts that recorded a read, which schedules them rather than running them. Then volunteer the boundaries, because that is what separates the model from the slogan: a read outside an observing context records nothing, an equal write is not a change, and mutation reached through a state object is invisible to it. If pushed on snapshot consistency, say plainly what it is and what it is not: it is about state objects rather than your own data structures, and it pins a reader to one version rather than making an update spread across several writes atomic.

lessons.title: `snapshotFlow` and Crossing Into Flow
lessons.summary: Sometimes the code that has to react to a UI value is not UI: an analytics call, a draft that saves itself, a request that follows the scroll position. `snapshotFlow` turns observable Compose state into a cold `Flow` a coroutine can process — what it evaluates and when, why its emissions are not a record of everything that happened, and where the collector's lifetime comes from.

blocks.text: Every consumer so far has had the same shape: a composable that reads state and describes UI from it. Some consumers are not that. An analytics event should be sent the first time the user scrolls past the top of a list. A draft should be saved a second after typing stops. A search request should be issued when the query settles. None of those describe UI, all of them need to know when a UI-owned value changed, and none of them can be a composable — composition is for describing, not for doing.
What that kind of consumer wants is a stream it can filter, transform, delay and suspend on. Kotlin already has one, `Flow`, and `snapshotFlow` is the adapter between the two worlds.

Four facts about `Flow` are enough for this lesson to stand on its own. The full subject is taught by the Flow Fundamentals unit of this curriculum: the first two facts are its treatment of cold flows, and the last two its treatment of collection lifetime and cancellation, both linked below. Operators, hot streams and sharing, and back pressure follow in the units after it.

items: **A cold flow produces nothing until it is collected.** The code inside the builder does not run when the flow is created. It runs when a collector arrives, and each new collector starts an independent execution.

**Collection is what starts it.** `collect` is a suspending call, so it needs a coroutine, and it does not return until the flow completes or the coroutine is cancelled. A `snapshotFlow` never completes on its own.
**The collector's lifetime is the coroutine's lifetime.** Whatever launched the collecting coroutine is what decides how long collection lasts.
**Stopping collection means cancelling that coroutine.** Collection stops and the `snapshotFlow` unsubscribes from the state it had been watching. There is nothing to dispose by hand.

blocks.text: With that in place, `snapshotFlow { }` is short to describe. It takes a block, and:

items: when collection begins it runs the block once and emits the result, unconditionally — the first value does not wait for anything to change;
while the block runs, it records which snapshot state the block read, which makes the block an observing context in exactly the sense of the previous lesson;
when a change is applied to any state the block read, it runs the block again and records the reads again;
it emits the new result only if that result is not equal to the last one it emitted. The documentation compares this to `distinctUntilChanged`, and the comparison really is `equals`.

blocks.text: `firstVisibleItemIndex` is snapshot state owned by the list state, and it is read **inside** the block. That is the whole reason it becomes a dependency: the block is the observing context, and the read happened while the block was running. Everything after `snapshotFlow` in that chain is ordinary `Flow`, doing ordinary `Flow` things.

`snapshotFlow` is the previous lesson's model with a different kind of dependent attached. The block plays the part the composable played: it reads state while something is recording, so a reported change re-runs it. What is new is only the destination — instead of invalidating a scope that will describe UI, the result travels to a coroutine as a `Flow` value.

A cold flow needs a collector, and the collector needs a coroutine whose lifetime is tied to the UI that produced the value. Inside composition that is `LaunchedEffect`: it launches a coroutine when it enters the Composition, cancels that coroutine when it leaves, and — if it is recomposed with different keys — cancels the running one and launches a new one. That is as much as this lesson needs; the effect APIs as a family, and how to choose between them, are a later unit's subject.

The keys in `LaunchedEffect(listState, analytics)` are doing real work, and getting them wrong is a correctness bug rather than a style point. The coroutine captures both values, and a captured value stays frozen for as long as that coroutine lives — the same capture problem `remember` and `derivedStateOf` have. In the snippet above `listState` comes from `rememberLazyListState()`, so it is stable for the life of that call site, while `analytics` is a parameter a caller can change at any recomposition: keyed only on `listState`, the effect would go on reporting to the `Analytics` it captured first. Hoist that list state to a caller and the mirror-image failure becomes possible too — an effect still watching the previous list's scroll position. The rule transfers without having to work out which holders happen to be stable today: key on every holder the effect must not outlive.
The mistake that produces the most confusing behaviour, though, is not about keys. It is about which side of the block the state is read on.

This compiles, it runs, and it emits exactly one value and then nothing ever again. By the time the block sees `index` it is an ordinary `Int`; the read that could have recorded a dependency happened in the composable, so the block reads no snapshot state at all. Measured on this project's JVM target: a block returning a captured plain value evaluated once, emitted once, and was never evaluated again after the underlying state changed. Note what this does *not* say — capturing a value is not a defect in itself and an ordinary captured value is not somehow half-observable. It is simply not observable. There is also a second, quieter cost here: the composable now reads `firstVisibleItemIndex` itself, so it is invalidated by every scrolled row, which is precisely what routing the value through a flow was supposed to avoid.
A subtler version of the same question arrives as soon as the state is a snapshot-aware collection, and it is worth being explicit about because the intuitive code is the wrong code.

The first block returns the `SnapshotStateList` reference without reading its contents, so two things go wrong at once and either alone would be fatal. No element read is recorded, so a change to the list never re-runs the block; and if it did re-run, the value it produced would be the same object it produced last time, equal to itself, so the emission would be suppressed anyway. Measured on this project's JVM target: adding an element after collection began produced no further evaluation and no further emission. The second block calls `toList()`, which reads the contents — creating the dependency — and returns an immutable list that genuinely differs from the previous one; the same measurement gave two evaluations and two emissions. This is not a trick to memorise: the runtime's own documentation for `SnapshotStateList.toList()` recommends it specifically for returning the value of the list from a `snapshotFlow`, and records that it is an O(1) operation returning the immutable list used internally rather than copying anything.
With that settled, the comparison people actually reach for — `snapshotFlow` or `derivedStateOf`? — turns out not to be a close call, because the two are not competing for the same job.

rows: Who consumes the result
Composition — a composable reads it
A coroutine — a collector receives it
What it produces
A `State<T>`
A cold `Flow<T>`
What it is for
Keeping a reading scope from being invalidated while the answer is unchanged
Applying stream processing — `map`, `filter`, `debounce`, suspend calls — to a changing value
What starts it
Reading the value
Collecting the flow
Where it lives
In the Composition, held by a `remember`
In a coroutine, held by whatever launched it

blocks.text: The single question that decides between them is who is on the other end. If a composable is going to read the answer, you want observable state and `derivedStateOf` is the tool that can filter its invalidations. If a coroutine is going to process the answer, you want a stream. Two things are true of both and worth saying out loud: neither is a persistence mechanism — nothing either produces outlives the Composition or the coroutine holding it — and neither moves work to another thread for you. A `snapshotFlow` collector runs in whatever context its coroutine was given, so if the work it does is not safe on the main thread, arranging a dispatcher is your job.

Using `snapshotFlow` as a record of what happened. It is a stream of *states*, not of *events*, and the runtime's documentation is unusually direct about the difference: state changes are conflated, only the most recent state matters, and an observer may legitimately skip intermediate values or see the same value twice. If a value moves through 0, 1, 2, 3 faster than the collector is scheduled, seeing only 0 and 3 is correct behaviour rather than a dropped event. Anything that must record every transition — an undo stack, an audit trail, a keystroke log — has to be fed where the change is made, not observed afterwards.
Evaluations of the block, writes to the state, and emissions to the collector are three different counts, and expecting them to line up is where most of the surprising behaviour comes from.

Measured on this project's JVM target, with the collector already running before any change was made and each change allowed to be applied and the scheduler allowed to settle before the next one, unless a row says otherwise:

items: A block returning an `Int` state: one evaluation and one emission when collection began, then one evaluation and one emission for the change that followed.
The same block, then assigned the value the state already held: no evaluation and no emission at all. An equal write is not a change, so nothing was ever reported.

A block returning `index > 2`, with the index driven through 1, 2, 3 and 4: five evaluations and two emissions. Every reported change re-ran the block; only the two results that differed from the previous one were emitted.

The `Int` block of the first row again, with 1, 2 and 3 written with no opportunity to settle in between: two evaluations and two emissions, the second carrying 3. The values 1 and 2 were read by nobody.

blocks.text: The first and last rows use the identical block, and the only difference between them is whether each write was allowed to be applied before the next one was made — which is what decides whether the collector sees every value or only the latest. Those numbers therefore describe when things were observed at least as much as they describe the code, which is why the runtime's documentation declines to promise any of them: the block "may run more than once for equal sets of inputs or only once after many rapid snapshot changes".

That sentence is also the reason for the constraint on what the block may contain. Because it can run an unpredictable number of times, it must be idempotent and free of side effects — and Compose enforces the strong half of that rather than trusting you with it. The block runs inside a read-only snapshot, and writing snapshot state from within it fails collection with an `IllegalStateException`; running that case on this project's JVM target produces exactly that, with the message `Cannot modify a state object in a read-only snapshot`. Which rules out the tempting debugging move of counting evaluations by incrementing a counter held in state. Keep the calculation a calculation and do the work in the collector, where side effects belong.

The deeper framing behind all of it is in the runtime's own words, and it is a good thing to be able to say: observable state is a lossy compression of the events that produced it. An event happens at a point in time and every one of them may carry meaning, so an observer of events must see all of them. State is only ever the latest value, so an observer of state has to be able to arrive late and still be correct. `snapshotFlow` models snapshot changes as events, but what it is observing is state, so the events it can offer are conflated by construction. That is a property of the thing being observed, not a limitation waiting to be worked around.

Expect the identification question — which API turns Compose `State` into a cold `Flow` — and answer it, but do not stop there, because it tests recall rather than understanding. Say what the block is: an observing context whose reads become the flow's dependencies, which is why the state has to be read *inside* it rather than captured from outside. Say what governs emission: the block re-runs on a reported change and emits only when its result is not equal to the previous one. Say where collection lives and what ends it: a coroutine, usually launched by `LaunchedEffect` and keyed on the holders it captures, cancelled when that effect leaves the Composition. Then give the boundary unprompted — conflated states rather than an event log — because that is the reasoning that decides whether `snapshotFlow` is the right tool for the problem in front of you.

units.title: Coroutine Fundamentals and Structured Concurrency
units.summary: Nearly every hard defect in asynchronous Android code comes from the same place: nobody can say what a piece of work's lifetime is. This unit builds the model that makes that answerable, in the order the ideas depend on one another. Suspension explains what a coroutine can do that a thread cannot; builders explain how work starts and what handle the caller gets back; `Job` gives that work an observable lifetime and a position in a hierarchy; `CoroutineScope` says who owns it; and structured concurrency turns ownership and hierarchy into guarantees a caller can rely on. Where code actually runs, how cancellation works, and what a failure does are deliberately later units — all three assume this material.

lessons.title: Suspension Is Not Blocking
lessons.summary: The most damaging misconception in this subject is that `suspend` means the work happens somewhere else. It does not. `suspend` is a statement about how a function may pause and says nothing about which thread runs it, which is why deciding whether a suspending call is safe on the main thread means opening it and reading what is inside.

blocks.text: Almost every interesting program spends most of its life waiting — for a response, for a file, for a timer, for the user to do something. What the machine does with that waiting time is the question this whole subject exists to answer, and there are only two broad answers to it.

One sentence of background makes the contrast work. A **thread** is a unit of execution the operating system schedules: it owns a call stack, costs memory measured in megabytes, and the JVM can typically keep a few thousand of them alive at once. Threads are how a program does more than one thing, and they are a finite resource that something eventually has to hand back.

**Blocking** is the first answer to waiting: the thread sits on the call until it returns. The thread is not doing work during that time, but it is also unavailable to anybody else. **Suspending** is the second: the coroutine pauses and the thread it was running on is released. Kotlin's documentation states it directly — coroutines "can suspend their execution instead of blocking a thread", which "allows one coroutine to suspend while waiting for some data to arrive and another coroutine to run on the same thread".

`suspend` is the keyword that marks a function as allowed to pause that way. It is a compile-time contract with two consequences and no others: the function may contain suspension points, and it can only be called from another suspending function or from a coroutine builder. That is the entire promise.

Everything people commonly read into the keyword is absent from it. `suspend` does not pick a thread or a thread pool. It does not move work into the background. It does not make a slow call fast, and it cannot change what the code inside the function actually does. A suspending function is perfectly free to sit on a thread for a second and never pause at all.

Both functions are marked `suspend` and the compiler is equally happy with both. Only one of them suspends. `delay` is documented as delaying a coroutine for at least the given time "without blocking a thread"; `Thread.sleep` holds the thread for the whole second. The keyword did not make the second behave like the first, and nothing in either signature tells them apart. (`Thread.sleep` is a JVM API, so that pair is a JVM and Android example — but the point it makes, that a blocking call inside a suspending function is still a blocking call, is not platform-specific.)

One sentence of mechanism is worth having and no more than one. A suspended coroutine is a stored **continuation** — the point to resume from, plus the local state needed to resume there — rather than a parked thread with a stack. That is why a suspended coroutine costs almost nothing, and why the thread can be handed to somebody else while it waits. How the compiler produces that continuation is not something any decision in your code depends on.

`suspend` describes how a function is allowed to pause. It does not describe where the function runs, and it cannot change what the code inside it does. A suspending function full of blocking calls blocks exactly as much as the same code would without the keyword.
Reading asynchronous code well means keeping three questions apart, because they have three different answers and only the first one is visible in a signature.

items: **Is this function allowed to suspend?** The `suspend` modifier answers this, and only this.

**Does this call actually block?** Only the code inside it can tell you. A suspending function that wraps a blocking API blocks; a suspending function that awaits a genuinely asynchronous one does not.
**Where does this run?** A separate question again, answered by the coroutine's dispatcher rather than by anything on the function.

blocks.text: The third question has a unit of its own and is deliberately left there. For now it is enough to know that the **dispatcher** is the part of a coroutine's configuration that decides which thread or thread pool runs it, that a coroutine inherits one rather than choosing one per call, and that nothing about the `suspend` keyword participates in that decision. Choosing dispatchers, and the damage a wrong choice does, is the next unit's subject.
That leaves the question you actually have to answer in front of real code: is this call safe from the main thread? Two functions with the same shape can have opposite answers.

The difference is invisible from the call site, which is why main-safety is treated as the obligation of the function being called rather than of the caller. Android's guidance states it in as many words: suspending functions "should be **main-safe**, meaning they're safe to call from the main thread", and a class that performs long-running blocking operations "must move execution off the main thread" itself. Read that for what it is — a **convention** about whose job main-safety is. Nothing enforces it: `readSettings` above breaks the convention and compiles perfectly, and no warning anywhere will mention it. So a `suspend` signature tells you what its author was supposed to have done, never what they did, and on a function you have not read the only way to find out is to open it.

The cost of getting this wrong is easy to make visible. Measured on this project's JVM target, on a dispatcher backed by a single thread: two coroutines each running `Thread.sleep(300)` took **607 ms** in total, while two coroutines each running `delay(300)` took **310 ms**. The blocking pair could not overlap, because there was one thread and the first coroutine never gave it up. On Android that thread is often the one drawing frames.

"I made it `suspend`, so it is off the main thread." Adding the keyword changes what the compiler permits and nothing about where the code runs; if the body was blocking the main thread before, it still is. The habit that replaces the belief is small: when you want to know whether a call is safe on the main thread, open it and look at what it does, and keep going until you reach either a genuinely suspending API or something that moves the work itself.

The reason suspension is worth a language feature is arithmetic. A waiting coroutine costs a continuation; a waiting thread costs a stack. Kotlin's own comparison runs 50,000 tasks that each wait five seconds: as coroutines that is roughly 500 MB, and as JVM threads it can reach 100 GB — far enough past the limit that the thread version may simply fail to start. "Many concurrent operations" is a design option in one model and an impossibility in the other.

Keeping the word "blocking" precise matters here, because two different things get called by that name and collapsing them removes the ground the next unit stands on. A **blocking call** holds a thread that is doing nothing — waiting on a socket, a lock, a sleep. A **CPU-bound loop** holds a thread that is doing work as fast as it can. They share one consequence, that the thread is unavailable and the coroutine reaches no suspension point, and they need different answers, which is exactly why the dispatchers unit separates the pools they belong on.

The shared consequence is worth seeing rather than believing. Measured the same way: on a single-thread dispatcher, a coroutine running a 250 ms busy loop finished entirely before a second coroutine launched onto the same dispatcher started at all. Nothing had gone wrong and nothing was misconfigured; there was simply no moment at which the first coroutine offered the thread back.

That points at a second consequence, which the cancellation unit later builds on. Cancellation in Kotlin is **cooperative**: a coroutine finds out it has been cancelled where it suspends at a cancellable point, or where its own code deliberately looks. A coroutine that does neither runs to the end regardless of what anybody else has asked for — the request is recorded and simply never observed. Where those checks belong, what they cost, and what a cancelled coroutine may still do are the third unit's subject rather than this one's.

"What does `suspend` do?" has a wrong answer that sounds right — "it runs the function in the background" — and interviewers ask it because the wrong answer is so common. Give the contract: the function may pause at a suspension point without holding its thread, and it can only be called from another suspending function or a builder. Then volunteer the boundary before you are pushed to it: the keyword chooses no thread and no dispatcher, and a suspending function that wraps a blocking call is not main-safe. If you can add why the model exists — a suspended coroutine costs a continuation rather than a stack — you have answered the follow-up too.

lessons.title: Starting Coroutines: `launch`, `async` and `runBlocking`
lessons.summary: A suspending function cannot start itself, so somewhere the chain has to begin. Three builders begin it, and they differ in what the caller receives and what the caller is able to do next — a handle, a future value, or a blocked thread. Choosing between them is a statement of intent that every later reader of the code will believe.

blocks.text: Suspension explains what a coroutine is able to do. It does not explain how one starts, and by itself it cannot: a suspending function can only be called from another suspending function, so the chain has to begin somewhere outside it. **Coroutine builders** are where it begins.

Three of them cover almost everything you will write. The useful way to tell them apart is not what they do to the work — all three run the block as a coroutine — but what they hand back and what the caller can do the instant afterwards.

rows: `launch`
the work has to happen and there is no result to return
`Job`
immediately, while the coroutine runs
`async`
the work produces a value somebody is going to consume
`Deferred<T>`
immediately; `await()` suspends until the value is ready
`runBlocking`
non-coroutine code has to call suspending code and there is no scope to launch into
whatever the block returns
only once the coroutine and everything launched in it has finished

blocks.text: `CoroutineScope.launch()` "starts a new coroutine without blocking the rest of the scope", and the documentation's own advice on when to use it is a description of intent rather than of mechanism: "to run a task alongside other work when the result isn't needed or you don't want to wait for it". It returns a `Job` handle, which the next lesson is about.

`CoroutineScope.async()` "starts a concurrent computation inside an existing coroutine scope and returns a `Deferred` handle that represents an eventual result", and `await()` is how you get that result: it suspends "until the result is ready". For this lesson that is the whole of `async` — it is the builder that gives you a value back.

`runBlocking` is the odd one out, and it is odd on purpose. It "creates a coroutine scope and blocks the current thread until the coroutines launched in that scope finish", and Kotlin's guidance for it is unusually blunt: use it "only when there is no other option to call suspending code from non-suspending code". Its API documentation is specific about where that is — it is "designed to bridge regular blocking code to libraries that are written in suspending style, to be used in `main` functions, in tests, and in non-`suspend` callbacks when `suspend` functions need to be called".

`launch` and `async` are extension functions on `CoroutineScope`, which is why neither can be called from nowhere: every coroutine they start belongs to something. `runBlocking` creates a scope of its own, and that is exactly what makes it a bridge rather than a fourth way of starting work inside code that already has one. As for the `{ }` after each call, that is an ordinary Kotlin trailing lambda — these are functions whose last parameter is itself a function, so the argument moves outside the parentheses, and `launch(dispatcher) { }` is the same shape with one ordinary argument in front.

Pick the builder from the intent, not from the shape of the surrounding code. `launch` says "this has to happen and there is nothing to hand back". `async` says "this produces a value I am going to use". `runBlocking` says "I am not in coroutine code, and I am willing to stop this thread until I am".
The first mistake is quiet. It compiles, it works, and it misinforms everybody who reads it afterwards.

Both run `save`, and the second is better code for a reason that has nothing to do with speed. `async` returns a `Deferred`, and a `Deferred` is a claim that somebody is going to ask for the outcome. Dropping it means the author either did not know that or did not mean it, and the next reader has to work out which — usually while looking for a bug elsewhere. `launch` states the intent exactly, and the type system stops implying anything else.

There is a second half to this that the failure unit owns. `async` stores its outcome in the `Deferred`, and a failure is an outcome, so an unconsumed `Deferred` is also an unread failure. What that failure then does to the rest of the coroutine tree is a question about propagation and supervision, and it is deliberately not answered here. The builder choice is worth making correctly on the intent argument alone.

The second mistake is loud, and the useful skill is predicting it from the definition rather than remembering a rule about it. `runBlocking` blocks the calling thread until its coroutine finishes. On Android's main thread, that thread is the one that draws frames, dispatches touches and runs lifecycle callbacks, so for the duration of the call the app renders nothing and responds to nothing; long enough and the system raises an ANR. Measured on this project's JVM target, `runBlocking { delay(300) }` returned to its caller after **306 ms**: suspending inside the block changed nothing whatsoever for the thread outside it, which is the entire point of a bridge.

Treating `runBlocking` as "the way to call a suspending function". It is not a converter from suspending to ordinary code; it is a thread being spent to wait. Inside a suspending function it is redundant by construction — the documentation's own example labels it "redundant and blocks the thread, avoid this", because you already had the ability to suspend and gave it away, "potentially leading to thread starvation issues". When `runBlocking` looks necessary in application code, the thing actually missing is a scope.

The interesting difference between `launch` and `async` is not the return type, it is the obligation the return type creates. A `Job` answers "is it still running, and has it finished?". A `Deferred` answers that and also "what did it produce?" — so choosing `async` adds a question somebody is expected to ask. Code that never asks it has an unmet obligation sitting in plain sight, which is why the unconsumed `Deferred` reads as a defect even before anything goes wrong.

Two things are deliberately absent from the builder list, and naming them is what stops them creeping in. **`withContext` is not a builder.** It starts no coroutine; it is a suspending function that runs a block with a changed context and returns the block's result. Filing it alongside `launch` and `async` is precisely how people come to believe it "starts something", and telling it apart from the scope builders is the next unit's job. And **`async` is not a parallelism feature here** — in this lesson it is the builder that returns a value, nothing more. Deciding when work should genuinely overlap, and what overlapping is worth, is a separate decision made later.

One parameter is worth recognising without reaching for it: both builders accept a `CoroutineStart`, and `CoroutineStart.LAZY` produces a coroutine that does not begin until its handle is started or awaited. It exists, it is occasionally the right tool, and it is not part of the intent decision this lesson is about.

The deeper reading of `runBlocking` is that blocking is a property of the *caller's thread* rather than of the coroutine. Nothing inside the block behaves differently; the coroutine suspends and resumes exactly as it would anywhere else. What differs is that one thread has been assigned to stand there until the whole thing is over. That is a defensible trade at a process boundary — a `main` function, a test, a callback that cannot suspend — and indefensible on a thread that has other obligations, and the same sentence explains both cases.

"What is the difference between `launch` and `async`?" invites the weak answer, "`async` returns a value". Say that and then say the thing behind it: the builder records the intent, `launch` for work with no result to hand back and `async` for a computation whose `Deferred` somebody is expected to consume, so `async { }` with a dropped handle is a statement the code does not mean. Expect a `runBlocking` follow-up, and answer it with the consequence rather than the word "bad": it blocks the calling thread until the coroutine completes, which is what you want in a `main` function or a test and what causes a frozen UI on the main thread.

lessons.title: `Job`: the Handle That Carries Lifetime
lessons.summary: `launch` returns a `Job` and most call sites throw it away, which makes it easy to read as a formality. It is the opposite: the `Job` is where a coroutine's lifetime becomes something anybody can ask questions about, and it is the edge that attaches a coroutine to its parent and its children.

blocks.text: Every coroutine has a `Job`. `launch` returns one directly; `async` returns a `Deferred`, which its documentation defines as "a `Job` with a result". The `Job` documentation's own one-line definition is worth keeping: "a job is a cancellable thing with a lifecycle that concludes in its completion". The useful reading of that is that a `Job` **is** the coroutine's lifetime, turned into an object you can hold.
Holding it lets you do three things, and they are the reasons the builders return it at all.

items: **Wait for it.** `join()` "suspends the coroutine until this job is complete", and it "resumes normally (without exception) when the job is complete for any reason".
**Ask about it.** `isActive`, `isCompleted` and `isCancelled` report which part of the lifecycle the job is currently in.
**Locate it in the tree.** A job knows its `parent` and can list its `children`, because jobs "can be arranged into parent-child hierarchies".

blocks.text: The parent-child link is not something you have to set up. A coroutine inherits its parent from the context it is started in, so a coroutine started inside another coroutine becomes that coroutine's child, and a coroutine started from a scope becomes a child of that scope's job. That inheritance is the default and it is what essentially all code relies on; it is also the mechanism underneath everything the last lesson of this unit describes. It can be overridden — passing a `Job` explicitly to a builder re-parents that coroutine out of the scope that launched it, which is a trap worth knowing about and the context unit's to take apart. Nothing in this unit does it.

Discarding the returned `Job` is normal and usually right. It is returned for the cases that need it, not as something every call has to consume: you keep it when you have to wait for exactly this piece of work, when something else has to be able to stop it, or when you want to report on whether it is still going.

One more fact belongs here in a single sentence, because the next unit builds on it. The `Job` is also an element of the coroutine's **context**, alongside things such as the dispatcher — that is how a new coroutine finds the right parent without anybody passing one around by hand. What a context is and what a child inherits from it is the next unit's first lesson.
The builder call starts the work. The `Job` is what lets anyone afterwards say anything true about that work: whether it is still running, when it actually finished, and what it is attached to.
Here is the case worth predicting before reading the answer, because the intuitive prediction is wrong and the correct one is the whole point of the parent-child link.

The parent's block has run to the end. It is nevertheless not complete, because it has a child that is not finished. Measured on this project's JVM target at the 100 ms mark: `isActive` was `true`, `isCompleted` was `false`, the job reported exactly one child, and printing the job itself gave `StandaloneCoroutine{Completing}`. After `parent.join()` returned, `isCompleted` was `true`.

**Completing** is a real state and it exists for exactly this situation. In the documentation's words: "Completion of an active coroutine's body ... transitions the job to the completing state. It waits in the completing state for all its children to complete before transitioning to the completed state." A parent finishing its own work and a parent finishing are two different events, and only the second one is what anybody waiting actually cares about.

Reading "the `launch` block returned" as "the coroutine finished". They are different moments whenever the block started anything, and the gap between them is where "the function returned but the work was still running" bugs live. The end of the block is not observable from outside; completion is, and the `Job` is the thing that tells them apart.

`Deferred<T>` is the same object with a value attached — the documentation calls it "a non-blocking cancellable future" with "the same state machine as `Job`". Everything above applies to it: it has a parent, it can have children, it can be joined. `await()` is the version of `join()` that also hands back what the computation produced, suspending without blocking the thread while it waits, and rethrowing if the computation failed instead of completing — where such a failure travels next is the failure unit's subject. A `Deferred` you have joined but not awaited has finished; you have simply not asked what it made.

One further thing a `Job` carries deserves naming here and nothing more than naming. Cancellation travels along these same parent-child edges, and the `Job` is the handle through which it is requested. How cancellation actually behaves — that it is cooperative rather than forced, what code has to do to honour it, what happens to cleanup — is the third unit's entire subject, and nothing in this unit depends on the answer. Until then, treat cancellation as a relationship the structure carries rather than a mechanism you have met.

The full state list is worth knowing because it explains the two transient states, which is where all of the interesting behaviour is. `New` is an optional initial state and `Active` is the default one.

blocks.text: Two readings of that table matter. **Completing is indistinguishable from Active from outside**, and that is correct rather than an omission: to anybody waiting, a job that is waiting for its children is still running, and there is nothing useful to tell apart. And **`isCompleted` is true for both final states**, which is why "did it finish?" and "did it succeed?" are separate questions — `isCancelled` is the property that separates them.

`isActive` is used here strictly as a question about state. The same property appears in the cancellation unit for a different purpose — deciding whether a loop should keep going — and that use carries rules this unit does not cover. Keeping the two apart avoids importing an answer before the question has been posed.

There is also a reason to prefer `join()` over any of the predicates when you actually need to coordinate. Each property is a statement about a moment that has already passed by the time your next line runs, so polling a job to decide what to do is a race by construction. Waiting for a transition and sampling a state are different operations, and only one of them gives an answer that is still true when you act on it.

Taken together, this is what makes the `Job` more than a receipt. The builder call tells you work started; the job tells you where that work sits in a hierarchy, whether the hierarchy is finished, and — because a parent waits — lets a single handle stand for an entire sub-tree of work you never named.

"What does `launch` return, and why would you keep it?" The complete answer has two halves. The handle half: a `Job` lets you wait with `join()`, ask whether the work is still running, and stop it. The structural half, which is the one that distinguishes a strong answer: a `Job` is also that coroutine's position in a tree, so waiting on a parent waits for everything it started. If you can describe the completing state — the body has finished, a child has not, so the parent is not complete — you have stated the guarantee the structure actually makes.

lessons.title: `CoroutineScope` and Who Owns a Coroutine's Lifetime
lessons.summary: Every coroutine's lifetime belongs to something, and a scope is that something. The question worth practising on any piece of asynchronous code is which object owns the work and what event ends that ownership — including, concretely rather than stylistically, what goes wrong when the honest answer is "nothing in particular".

blocks.text: A `CoroutineScope` is described by its own documentation as "a scope in which coroutines run" that "allows managing the lifecycles of several coroutines simultaneously". The word carrying the weight in that sentence is *lifecycles*. A scope is not a convenience object that happens to provide `launch`; it is the thing a coroutine's lifetime is attached to.

Mechanically a scope is a very thin thing. The `CoroutineScope` interface declares exactly one property, `coroutineContext`, and no functions at all — `launch` and `async` are extensions on it. So a scope **holds** a `CoroutineContext` rather than being one, and the element of that context which matters here is the `Job` from the previous lesson. Launching from a scope makes the scope's job the parent of the new coroutine, and the identity is checkable rather than metaphorical:

Two consequences follow, and between them they are the whole lesson. Cancelling a scope cancels everything launched in it, recursively — "if a scope is cancelled, all coroutines in it are cancelled too". And a scope "cannot be completed until all its children are completed". So a coroutine's lifetime is **bounded** by the scope it was launched from: most work finishes well before its scope does, and none of it can outlast the scope. The **owner** of a scope is whatever decides where that bound falls — for a scope you construct and hold, whoever calls `cancel()` on it; for a lexical scope, the end of the block itself. A scope that is never cancelled and never ends is a bound that never arrives, which is the failure the rest of this lesson is about.
That collapses a large amount of asynchronous-code review into a single question, and it is worth asking out loud rather than by feel.

**Who owns this coroutine, and what event ends its lifetime?** If the answer names something with a lifecycle — this screen, this view model, this session, this download — the work has an owner. If the answer is "it stops when it stops", it does not, and every failure in the rest of this lesson follows from that one fact.
Here is the shape with no owner. It is common, it compiles, it passes review regularly, and nothing about it looks wrong.

One element of that constructor call is a distraction and is worth setting aside explicitly. `SupervisorJob()` changes what a child's failure does to its siblings; it changes nothing about ownership, and the failure unit teaches it properly. The defect below is present with or without it.

The scope was created and is never cancelled, so its job stays active for as long as anything holds it — and the running coroutines hold it. What goes wrong is not one thing, which is why "it leaks" is an unhelpful summary:

items: Work carries on after whatever asked for it has gone. The search still hits the network, still parses, still writes to the database, for a screen the user closed two navigations ago.
Results land on state that no longer matters, so a stale response can overwrite a newer one or call back into an object that has already been torn down.
Everything the coroutine captured stays reachable for as long as the coroutine does — the controller, the repository, whatever the lambda closed over, and transitively whatever those hold.
A failure inside the coroutine surfaces detached from any lifecycle — a crash or a log line attributable to no screen, request or object in particular.
No caller can find out whether the work has finished, because nothing was returned and there is nothing to join.

blocks.text: The last of those is measurable. Measured on this project's JVM target: a suspending function whose body launched into a separately constructed scope returned to its caller after **5 ms** for work that took **300 ms**, and that work then completed normally long after the caller had moved on. Written as a structured child of the caller instead, the same body returned after **306 ms**. Both versions "work"; only one of them told the caller anything true.

The fix is ownership, not the removal of the constructor. `CoroutineScope(...)` is a legitimate way to build a scope — the documentation's own order of preference puts lexical scopes first and this constructor second, "for entity lifecycles", with the parenthetical that does all the work: *with required `cancel()` call*. Give the class a teardown point, cancel there, and the same code becomes correct.

Android supplies scopes whose owner is already defined, and `viewModelScope` is the one worth recognising as the shape to imitate: "a `ViewModelScope` is defined for each `ViewModel` in your app. Any coroutine launched in this scope is automatically canceled if the `ViewModel` is cleared." The lifetime is a real event in a real object's lifecycle and the class launching work does not have to remember anything. Note what that is an example *of* — ownership done well — rather than an instruction about where coroutines belong; what a view model should contain is the architecture curriculum's subject, not this one's.

Some work genuinely has to outlive the screen that started it: a bookmark write, an upload that should not be abandoned because the user navigated away. That is not a reason to have no owner, it is a reason to have a longer-lived one. Android's guidance is to inject a scope whose lifetime is deliberately longer rather than reaching for a global one, so that the longer lifetime is a decision recorded in a constructor parameter and can be replaced in a test. Work that must survive the process being killed is not a coroutine problem at all — that is what a durable scheduler such as WorkManager exists for, and no scope of any lifetime will do it.

"Never create your own `CoroutineScope`" is the rule people take away, and it is the wrong lesson drawn from the right examples. The defect is never the constructor call. It is a scope with no cancellation point — a lifetime with no end, so work with no owner. A scope created in a class and cancelled in that class's teardown is correct, and a scope handed to you by a framework and then never cancelled by anybody would be broken in exactly the same way.

The reframing that survives contact with a real codebase is that a scope is a **lifetime declaration**, so the design question is which lifetime is the shortest one that is still long enough. Most work started from a screen wants the screen's. A cache several screens share wants something longer. Very little wants the process's.

`GlobalScope` is the process's, and the documentation says precisely what makes it a trap without banning it: it is "a `CoroutineScope` with the lifetime of the whole application", and "it is easy to misuse it and create memory or resource leaks when a coroutine actually should be tied to the lifecycle of some entity". Read the shape of that warning — the objection is to the *mismatch* between the work's natural lifetime and the scope's, not to the existence of a long-lived scope.

That leaves process-lifetime scopes a narrow but real use: state that genuinely is application-wide and has to survive every screen. What keeps such a scope honest is making it an injected dependency with a name and a documented reason, rather than a global reached from anywhere. That is also why Android's guidance frames its objection to `GlobalScope` in terms of testing and control: a hard-coded global scope cannot be substituted in a test, so the code cannot be told to stop — and "cannot be told to stop" is the same defect wearing different clothes.

One of the failures listed earlier — a failure surfacing with no lifecycle attached to it — is worth bounding, because it is easy to over-read. An un-owned coroutine's failure does not disappear — it surfaces somewhere, as a crash or as a log line — but it arrives detached from any lifecycle, so nothing identifies which screen, request or object it belonged to. That is a claim about diagnosability and nothing more. Where a coroutine failure actually travels, what can intercept it on the way, and how supervision changes that are the failure unit's subject; ownership does not settle them, and neither does this lesson.

One last consequence is worth stating because it is the reason the discipline pays for itself. When every coroutine has an owner, "stop everything this screen started" is one call rather than a search through the codebase for things to cancel. Ownership is not bookkeeping imposed on top of the work; it is the property that makes the work controllable at all.

Expect a short code sample and "what is wrong with this?". Answer with ownership rather than with a rule: name the scope, say what cancels it, and when nothing does, say what that means concretely — work continuing past the screen, stale results landing on dead state, captured objects retained, failures surfacing with no lifecycle attached to them, and no way for a caller to know it finished. If the follow-up is about work that must outlive the screen, do not retreat to `GlobalScope`: say the lifetime should be longer *and owned*, injected rather than reached for, and that surviving the process is a scheduler's job rather than a scope's.
