units.title: Cancellation, Failure and Coordination
units.summary: Units 1 and 2 built structured work and decided where it runs. This unit asks what happens when that work is stopped or goes wrong. Cancellation is a request that the code inside has to notice; cleanup and deadlines are expressed through the same request; a failure travels through the same hierarchy that carries lifetime; supervision changes exactly one relationship in that hierarchy; and concurrent work that all succeeds can still corrupt the state it shares. The order is one argument rather than five API pages.

lessons.title: Cancellation Is Cooperative
lessons.summary: Decide whether a particular coroutine will actually stop when it is cancelled. Cancelling records a request on the Job; the coroutine observes that request only where it suspends cooperatively or checks explicitly, so a busy loop keeps running and a broad catch can consume the request altogether.

blocks.text: Unit 1 introduced cancellation as something the hierarchy carries and stopped there. This Lesson answers the question that was left open: after cancel() returns, has the work stopped? The honest answer is that cancelling is a request, and whether it takes effect depends on what the coroutine does next.

The sequence is worth holding as a picture. Cancellation is requested on a Job. The Job moves into its cancelling state. The coroutine keeps running until it reaches a point where cancellation can be observed. At that point a CancellationException is thrown, and the coroutine unwinds. Nothing in that chain forcibly stops arbitrary code.

The Kotlin documentation states the rule directly: coroutine cancellation is cooperative, and coroutines react to cancellation only when they cooperate by suspending or checking for cancellation explicitly. Cooperation is a property of the code inside the coroutine, not of the coroutine machinery around it.

Which suspending calls cooperate is more precise than it first looks. Every suspending function in the kotlinx.coroutines library cooperates, because they are built on suspendCancellableCoroutine, which checks for cancellation when the coroutine suspends. A custom suspending function written on top of the plain suspendCoroutine does not react to cancellation at all. Marking a function suspend is a signature, not a behaviour: it does not insert a cancellation check anywhere.

The loop above ignores cancellation completely, and wrapping performCpuWork in a suspend function would change nothing unless that function itself suspends or checks. It is also worth noticing what cancel() does for the caller: it requests cancellation and returns immediately. The moment nothing is running is the moment the Job completes, which is a separate event.

Cancelling records a request on the Job. The coroutine stops where it observes that request, so the interesting question is never whether cancel() was called but whether the code reaches a cooperative point.

Long-running code that does not suspend has three ways to cooperate, and they are not interchangeable. isActive is a property that becomes false once cancellation is requested, so it fits a loop condition. ensureActive() throws a CancellationException if cancellation was requested, so it fits a statement inside a loop body where continuing would be wrong. yield() releases the thread to other coroutines as well as checking, so it fits code that would otherwise monopolise its dispatcher thread.

rows: isActive
Reads false once cancellation has been requested; throws nothing.
The loop should end normally and the surrounding code should carry on.
ensureActive()
Throws CancellationException when cancellation has been requested.
Continuing past this point would be wrong, so unwinding is the correct outcome.
yield()
Releases the thread to other coroutines and throws CancellationException if cancelled.
The work is long and CPU-bound, and holding the thread would starve other coroutines.

blocks.text: There is one more trap in the same area, and it is easy to miss because the code looks cooperative. A call to a suspending function is a suspension point, but it does not always suspend: awaiting a Deferred that has already completed, or a repository call that returns a cached value without waiting for anything, resumes without ever suspending. A loop whose only suspending call is served from a cache therefore has no cancellation check in practice, even though every line of it is suspend. When a loop must be interruptible, the check has to be something that always checks.

The structure carries the request downward. Cancelling a coroutine requests cancellation of its descendants, and each of them faces the same question about its own code. Cancelling a parent therefore does not mean its descendants have stopped; it means every one of them has been asked to. Waiting is a separate operation: join() suspends until a Job is complete, and cancelAndJoin() exists precisely because requesting and waiting are two steps.

Reading a cancelled scope as a stopped scope. After scope.cancel() returns, children may still be finishing their current step and running their cleanup. If a test or a shutdown path depends on the work being over, it has to wait for completion rather than for the request.

It is reasonable to ask why cancellation is not simply preemptive, given how much reasoning cooperation costs. The answer is that a preempted coroutine could be stopped in the middle of a mutation, halfway through updating two fields that are supposed to agree, or between acquiring a resource and recording that it must be released. Cooperative cancellation is what makes finally blocks and invariants meaningful at all. The price is exactly the gap this Lesson is about: cancelled means asked to stop, and the interval between the request and the stop is real time in which the coroutine is still running.

The second consequence is that CancellationException is not an application error. It belongs to coroutine control flow: it is how a cancelled coroutine unwinds, and the machinery treats it differently from a failure. That makes a broad handler dangerous in a specific way.

The problem is not the word Exception. The problem is that the handler consumed a cancellation and then continued as though the operation were healthy, so the loop runs another iteration, the retry fires, or a result is reported for work nobody wants any more. The rule worth carrying is narrower than never catch Exception: do not consume cancellation and proceed. The documentation's own advice is to rethrow it so cancellation propagates correctly, and the CoroutineExceptionHandler reference shows the same idea as a check inside the handler.

Cancellation is also distinct from failure in the other direction. A coroutine that ends with a CancellationException does not fail its parent, while a coroutine that ends with any other exception does. That asymmetry is the subject of the third Lesson in this Unit; here it is enough to know that the two are different categories rather than two names for the same event.

items: Cancelling requests cancellation on a Job and returns; completion is a separate event.
A coroutine observes the request at a cancellable suspension point or at an explicit check.
Library suspending functions cooperate because they are built on suspendCancellableCoroutine; the suspend keyword alone guarantees nothing.
isActive, ensureActive() and yield() are the three checks, and they suit different shapes of loop.
A handler that swallows CancellationException lets cancelled work carry on.

blocks.text: Given a coroutine that runs a CPU-bound loop, say what cancel() does to it and name the three ways to make it cooperative. Then explain what a broad catch (e: Exception) does to cancellation, without retreating to the slogan that Exception must never be caught.

lessons.title: Cleanup, `NonCancellable` and Timeouts
lessons.summary: Release resources correctly while a cancelled coroutine unwinds, and read a deadline as cancellation with a clock. Ordinary cleanup belongs in finally, suspending cleanup needs NonCancellable, and a timeout bounds only what is prepared to observe cancellation.

blocks.text: A cancelled coroutine does not vanish. It unwinds, which means the CancellationException travels out through the call stack and every finally block on the way runs. That is where cleanup belongs, and for ordinary non-suspending work it is enough: closing a handle, releasing a lock, restoring a flag, removing an entry from a map.

There is a subtlety before that, and the documentation gives it a name: prompt cancellation. When a suspended coroutine is cancelled, it resumes with a CancellationException instead of returning a value, even if that value is already available. This is deliberate, because it stops a cancelled screen from being updated with data that arrived a moment too late. It also means a call can produce a resource whose value never reaches the caller, so an assignment written at the call site never happens and nothing is left to close.

The remedy is more specific than declaring the variable earlier: the capture has to happen inside the block, into a variable the finally block can already see. Then the reference exists whether or not the block's result is delivered.

That covers the caller. It does not cover the case where you are writing the suspending function that hands the resource back, because a caller cannot close something it never received. There the release belongs at the point of resumption: the cancellable-continuation form of resume takes a handler that runs precisely when the value was not successfully used to resume the coroutine, which is what it exists for.

The second surprise is what happens when cleanup itself suspends. The coroutine is already cancelled, so a cancellable suspending call inside the finally block observes that cancellation immediately and throws instead of doing its work. A suspending close() written that way silently does nothing at all.

Ordinary cleanup belongs in finally and needs nothing special. Suspending cleanup in an already-cancelled coroutine needs withContext(NonCancellable), because otherwise it observes the cancellation and does nothing.

NonCancellable is easy to describe in a way that invites abuse. It is not a way to finish important work despite cancellation. It is an escape hatch for the narrow case where cleanup has to suspend, and its whole effect is to make that block deaf to cancellation. Anything long or arbitrary inside it is time during which the coroutine cannot be stopped, which is exactly the responsiveness the cancellation model exists to provide.

Three boundaries keep it honest. Keep the block small and cleanup-shaped: releasing a lease, flushing a buffer, sending a close frame. Do not put transactions, network calls or user-visible work in it. And use it only with withContext: the API reference warns that launch(NonCancellable) severs the parent-child relation entirely, so the parent neither waits for that child nor is cancelled when it crashes. It is also worth remembering that the code after the block is still running in a cancelled coroutine, so an ensureActive() afterwards is often what the author actually meant.

Timeouts are the same model with a clock attached. withTimeout runs its block and, at the deadline, cancels it with a TimeoutCancellationException; withTimeoutOrNull does the same and returns null instead of throwing. Nothing new happens at the deadline: cancellation is requested, and the block observes it wherever it is prepared to. The API reference is explicit that withTimeout behaves like coroutineScope, creating a new lexically scoped child coroutine, and that cancellation on timeout runs concurrently with the code in the block and may happen at any time, even after the block has finished but before the caller is resumed with the result.

Treating withTimeout as a hard deadline for the caller. It is a request to cancel the block at a moment in time. If the block cannot observe cancellation, the deadline passes and the work continues, and because the block is a structured child the caller waits for it.

That last claim is worth measuring rather than asserting, so it was. The cases below were run on this project's JVM target against the resolved kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0, each with a 100 ms deadline and withTimeoutOrNull. They are measurements on one machine, not API guarantees. For calibration, a cooperative delay(1500) under the same deadline returned in 171-212 ms on the same run, so roughly 100 ms of every figure below is harness overhead rather than coroutine behaviour.

rows: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1500) }
null
about 1.7 s
A 1500 ms CPU loop with no suspension point and no check
the computed value, not null
about 1.5 s
join() on a Job belonging to a separate, non-child scope
null, and that job was still active afterwards
about 0.2 s
The same blocking call wrapped in runInterruptible
null
about 0.2 s

blocks.text: The second row is the sharp one. The block outlived its deadline by roughly fifteen times and then succeeded: it never reached a cancellation check, so the timeout's cancellation was never observed and the computed value was returned as though nothing had happened. A reader who believes a timeout is a hard stop will not predict that. The first row is the same story with blocking work, and in both the caller waited the whole time, because the block is a lexically scoped child and structured completion does not let withTimeout return before it finishes.

The third row is the only case where the caller moves on at the deadline, and it does so precisely because the awaited work was never a child of the timeout. The unrelated job kept running afterwards. That is Unit 1's ownership argument arriving from a different direction: a deadline bounds the structure it owns, and work outside that structure is not bounded by it at all.

The fourth row is the JVM-specific escape hatch. Thread interruption is a JVM mechanism, and this is a Kotlin Multiplatform curriculum, so runInterruptible is not part of the coroutine cancellation model everywhere. On the JVM it bridges the two models: it runs a blocking block and interrupts its thread when the coroutine is cancelled, turning cancellation into the InterruptedException that blocking JVM APIs already understand, and converting that back into a CancellationException for the coroutine. Blocking calls on other targets have no equivalent, and no dispatcher interrupts threads on its own.

The general statement is therefore narrower than the API name suggests. A timeout only becomes effective where cancellation can be observed, and structured ownership decides who waits. Reaching for withTimeout around code that cannot cooperate produces a deadline that is documentation rather than behaviour; the fix is to make the work cancellable, to bridge it on the platform that allows bridging, or to accept that the operation is not interruptible and design around it.

items: Ordinary cleanup in finally runs as the cancelled coroutine unwinds.
Prompt cancellation can discard an already-available value: capture resources inside the block, and release them at the resume site when you write the producer.
Suspending cleanup after cancellation needs withContext(NonCancellable), kept small and cleanup-shaped.
A timeout is cancellation with a clock, and withTimeout's block is a lexically scoped child.
Non-cooperative work can outlive its deadline and even return a successful result.
runInterruptible is a JVM bridge to thread interruption, not universal coroutine behaviour.

blocks.text: Does withTimeout(100) guarantee that the call returns in about 100 ms? Answer with the mechanism: what the deadline requests, why the caller waits for a structured child, and what happens when the block never checks for cancellation.

lessons.title: How a Coroutine Failure Travels
lessons.summary: Look at a coroutine tree, pick the child that throws, and name everything else that changes. Cancellation and failure are different categories, launch and async differ in how a failure is reported rather than in whether it propagates, and a CoroutineExceptionHandler applies only where an exception has no propagation path.

blocks.text: Two things can end a coroutine early, and the model treats them differently. A CancellationException means this work was asked to stop; a coroutine that ends with it does not cancel its parent. Any other exception means this work failed; a coroutine that ends with one cancels its parent with that exception. The documentation states it in one sentence: when a coroutine is cancelled it terminates but does not cancel its parent, and if it encounters an exception other than CancellationException it cancels its parent with that exception.
From there the ordinary rules follow from Unit 1's hierarchy. Take a parent with three regular children, where B throws.

blocks.code:
Parent
 |- Child A
 |- Child B   <-- throws IllegalStateException
 |- Child C

blocks.text: B fails, so it cancels Parent with that exception. Parent, now cancelling, requests cancellation of its remaining children, so A and C are cancelled — as cancellation, not as failure, which is why they do not each report an error of their own. Parent is not complete at the moment B throws: it completes once every child has finished unwinding, and the exception is what it completes with. Where that exception then goes depends on Parent's own situation, which is the subject of the deeper section below.

Builders differ in one respect, and it is not whether failure propagates. The guide puts them in two flavours: propagating exceptions automatically, which is launch, or exposing them to the caller, which is async. A failing launch has nowhere to put its exception, so the structure carries it. A failing async stores its outcome in the Deferred, and await() rethrows it there.

Cancellation travels downward and does not fail a parent. A non-cancellation failure travels upward, cancels the parent, and takes the siblings with it. The builder decides where the failure can be observed, not whether it propagates.

The distinction between propagation and observation is where the common misconception lives. It is often summarised as async exceptions only mattering when await() is called, and that is false for a regular structured child.

The async coroutine is a child of the scope under ordinary Job rules, so its failure cancels that scope whether or not anyone holds the Deferred. What await() adds is observation: it is where the failure the Deferred represents reaches the awaiter as a thrown exception, so ordinary try/catch can deal with it. Dropping the Deferred hides the failure from the call site without preventing it from tearing the scope down, which is a harder bug than a crash.

Inside a launch, the normal answer is even simpler: catch the specific exception where it happens. A failure that is handled inside the coroutine never becomes a propagation question at all, because the machinery never learns about it. That is the first and most ordinary way an exception is dealt with, and reaching past it for a handler is usually a sign that the failure was expected rather than exceptional.

One detail matters when several children fail. The rule is that the first exception wins: it is the one that gets handled, and the ones that follow are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. Scope that second half to the platform before relying on it. The guide notes that the suppression mechanism currently works on Java 1.7 and above, and that the JS and Native restrictions are temporary — so on the JVM a log reporting only the first failure's message is telling a partial story and the suppressed list holds the rest, while on the other targets this curriculum builds for there is no guarantee the rest will be found there.
Believing an unawaited Deferred makes a failure irrelevant. It removes the place where the failure would have been observed, not the structural relationship that propagates it.

CoroutineExceptionHandler is the part of this Lesson worth stating precisely, because the natural summary — put one in your scope to catch coroutine errors — is exactly wrong. The API reference frames it as an element for handling coroutine exceptions without a clear propagation path, and it enumerates the paths it recognises.

items: The exception is caught by a try/catch inside the coroutine, so the machinery never learns about it.
The coroutine is lexically scoped, like coroutineScope or withContext, so the exception is rethrown to the caller.
The exception is transferred to a parent that processes child failures, through structured concurrency.
The builder returns a handle that allows querying the result, which is async and its Deferred.

blocks.text: When none of those applies, the exception has no propagation path, and only then is the handler in that coroutine's context invoked. The common cases with no path are a launch on a scope that has no Job, and a child launched directly in a supervisorScope or under a SupervisorJob — which is the subject of the next Lesson. If no handler is present the runtime falls back to a platform-specific last-resort behaviour, which differs per target and is not something a multiplatform application should depend on.

The handler above is never invoked because the failure does have a path: it cancels coroutineScope, which rethrows to the caller. Installing a handler on an ordinary child does not turn that child into an independent boundary; it only names a handler that the situation never consults. The reference makes the same point about nesting: a handler on an outer root coroutine runs and a handler on its ordinary inner child does not, because the failure was propagated normally and it was the outer coroutine that had nowhere left to send it.

Two limits are worth stating alongside. The handler cannot recover: it is called after the coroutine has completed with that exception, so it is for logging, reporting, or restarting, not for retrying. And CancellationException is ignored by all handlers, which is the same asymmetry as the first Lesson in this Unit, seen from the reporting side.

Finally, a boundary rather than a topic. Failures a system expects — a request that can legitimately return not-found, a parse that can legitimately fail — are often better modelled as values in the return type than as exceptions, and the architecture curriculum owns that argument. The point that belongs here is that the two are not interchangeable: modelling expected failures as results does not make unexpected coroutine exceptions go away, and a coroutine that throws still obeys everything above.

items: A non-cancellation failure cancels the parent, which cancels the siblings, and completes with that exception.
launch propagates automatically; async represents the failure in its Deferred, where await() observes it.
A dropped Deferred still fails its parent under ordinary Job rules.
The first exception wins; on the JVM the later ones arrive as suppressed exceptions, which JS and Native do not currently guarantee.
CoroutineExceptionHandler applies only to a failure with no propagation path, never to async, and never to an ordinary child.

blocks.text: Draw a small tree, fail one child, and narrate the consequences: parent state, sibling cancellation, where the exception ends up, and when the parent is considered complete. Then say why a handler attached to that child would never run.

lessons.title: `SupervisorJob`, `supervisorScope` and the Limits of Isolation
lessons.summary: Isolate independent failures without pretending they did not happen. Supervision reverses exactly one relationship at exactly one parent-child boundary, leaves downward cancellation intact, and hands each supervised child the responsibility for its own failure.

blocks.text: The previous Lesson established the ordinary rule: a child's failure cancels its parent, which cancels its remaining children. Supervision is the one exception to that rule, and it is narrower than it is usually remembered. The API reference for SupervisorJob puts it plainly: children of a supervisor job can fail independently of each other, and a failure or cancellation of a child does not cause the supervisor job to fail and does not affect its other children.

Read that as one arrow being reversed and nothing else changing. Cancellation still travels downward: cancelling the supervisor cancels its children, and if a SupervisorJob is given a parent of its own, it is an ordinary child of that parent and is cancelled when the parent fails or is cancelled, taking its own children with it. Supervision changes what a child's failure does to the parent, not what the parent's cancellation does to the children.

supervisorScope is the lexically scoped form: it runs a block in a new scope containing a SupervisorJob, based on the caller's context. A child launched in it that fails does not affect the other children. The scope still waits — its lifecycle completes when both the block and all the coroutines launched in it complete — and if the block itself finishes with an exception, that does cancel the scope and all its children.

blocks.code:
supervisorScope
 |- Child A
 |- Child B
     |- Grandchild C   <-- fails

blocks.text: The picture above is the one to be able to read. Supervision applies to the boundary between supervisorScope and its direct children, A and B. C is an ordinary child of B, so their relationship is unchanged: C's failure cancels B in the ordinary way. Supervision then stops the failure at the supervised boundary, so A keeps running. Nothing recursively converted B's Job into a supervisor.

Supervision is a property of one parent-child boundary. It stops a child's failure from reaching that parent and its siblings; it does not make children unfailable, does not reach nested children, and does not stop cancellation travelling down.

The problem supervision is for is genuinely independent work presented together. Three panels on a dashboard refresh from three sources; one source is down. Under a regular Job the failure cancels the parent and the other two panels lose their in-flight work for no reason. Under a supervised parent each refresh stands or falls alone.

The half that gets forgotten is what happens to the failure afterwards. Isolating siblings answers one question — should this child's failure cancel the others — and says nothing about what the application does with the failure. A supervised child's exception no longer has a parent that will process it, so, in the vocabulary of the previous Lesson, it has no propagation path. Somebody must give it one.

The reference lists the two ways, and they line up with the builders. A failure of a supervised child created with launch can be handled by a CoroutineExceptionHandler in the context — this is one of the few places where installing a handler genuinely takes effect, because the child really is a boundary. A failure of a supervised child created with async is handled by awaiting its Deferred. Local try/catch inside the child remains the most direct option and the one that allows a fallback rather than only a report.

Adding SupervisorJob to stop a crash. Supervision changes who is cancelled, not whether the failure happened. Used to silence an error, it converts a loud failure into a screen that quietly shows stale or half-correct data.

Unit 2 taught the context half of the launch(SupervisorJob()) trap: a Job passed as an argument is not merged into the hierarchy, it replaces the parent for that one coroutine. This is where the argument finishes.

Trace the Jobs. The fresh SupervisorJob becomes the parent of the coroutine that launch creates, replacing the scope's Job, so that coroutine is no longer a child of the scope: the scope will not wait for it and cancelling the scope will not cancel it. The coroutine itself still receives its own ordinary Job, and A and B are children of that ordinary Job. Their relationship to it is completely unsupervised, so if A fails it cancels their parent and B goes with it. The SupervisorJob supervises a boundary that has exactly one child — the launched coroutine — which is not the boundary anyone wanted.

It is worth saying plainly that this is an anti-pattern rather than a recipe with a caveat. If the goal is isolated siblings, supervise the boundary those siblings actually sit on: wrap them in a supervisorScope, or build the owning scope with a SupervisorJob so that everything launched from the scope is supervised. The library says the same thing from the other direction: the launch reference states that it is incorrect to pass a Job element in the context because doing so breaks structured concurrency, and the overload that accepts one is deprecated.

rows: supervisorScope { }
The scope and the coroutines launched directly in it.
Does not reach nested children, and does not survive the block itself throwing.
CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + ...)
The scope's Job and everything launched from that scope.
Does not supervise coroutines those children launch in turn.
launch(SupervisorJob())
A boundary with one child: the coroutine launch created.
Does not supervise that coroutine's own children, and detaches it from the scope.

blocks.text: The judgement underneath all of this is a design question rather than an API question. Supervision is a statement that these children are independent of one another. If they genuinely are — three panels, three uploads, three cached sources — isolating them is correct and the alternative is worse. If they are not, isolating them turns a clean, complete failure into a partially applied change or a screen showing data that no longer agrees with itself. The question to ask before reaching for it is not how to stop this failure cancelling everything, but whether this work is actually independent.

items: A supervised child's failure does not cancel the supervisor or its siblings.
Cancellation still travels down: cancelling a supervisor cancels its children.
supervisorScope supervises its direct children only, and still waits for all of them.
A supervised failure has no propagation path, so each child needs its own handling.
launch(SupervisorJob()) re-parents one coroutine and supervises nothing useful.

blocks.text: Given a nested launch inside a supervisorScope whose inner child fails, name every coroutine that is cancelled and say why. Then explain why launch(SupervisorJob()) does not isolate the siblings inside it, in terms of which Job became whose parent.

lessons.title: Shared Mutable State and Choosing a Coordination Mechanism
lessons.summary: Recognise state that two coroutines can touch at once and choose a mechanism for it on purpose. An atomic fits one independent value, confinement fits related state with one owner, and a Mutex fits a critical section that must stay consistent across several suspending steps.

blocks.text: Everything so far has been about one coroutine's lifetime. This Lesson is about what happens when several of them succeed at the same time and touch the same state on the way. Nothing about coroutines makes shared mutable state safe; a coroutine is a unit of work, not a unit of isolation.

The reason is that counter++ is not one indivisible operation. It reads the current value, adds one, and writes the result back. Two coroutines running on different threads can read the same value before either writes, and one increment is lost. The Kotlin guide's version of this example makes the same point and notes that it is highly unlikely ever to print the expected total.

What makes it possible is genuine multi-threaded execution, which is a platform property rather than a coroutine property. On the JVM, Android and Native, Dispatchers.Default really does run coroutines on several threads at once, so the race above is real. On JS and Wasm the runtime is single-threaded, so the same code cannot interleave that way — which is a reason to be careful about where an example is claimed to apply, not a reason to write shared mutable state and hope.

A common first attempt does not work either. Marking the variable volatile on the JVM makes reads and writes individually atomic and visible to other threads, but it does not make a read-modify-write sequence atomic, so the lost update survives. Visibility and atomicity are different problems. The three answers that do work are a thread-safe or atomic operation, confining the state to a single execution owner, and mutual exclusion with a Mutex.

Concurrency plus shared mutable state is a race, whatever the concurrency is made of. The choice is between making the operation atomic, giving the state one owner, or guarding the critical section — and the right answer depends on the shape of the state, not on taste.

An atomic fits when the state is one value and the update can be expressed as a single atomic operation. Kotlin's common atomics live in kotlin.concurrent.atomics and are available from commonMain on Kotlin 2.4.10, behind an opt-in: the API is still marked @ExperimentalAtomicApi, so a usage needs @OptIn or the matching compiler argument. Note also what the API documentation says about targets — on JS and Wasm the implementation is trivial and not thread-safe, because those platforms do not support multi-threading.

The limit of an atomic is the word one. An atomic counter is a correct counter; two atomics are not a correct pair. If the invariant is that a list and its size agree, or that a balance and a transaction log are updated together, making each field atomic protects each field and protects nothing about the relationship between them. That is the point at which an atomic is the wrong tool rather than an incomplete one.

Confinement inverts the question. Instead of coordinating everyone who touches the state, run every mutation on one execution owner so that they cannot overlap in the first place. What makes it confinement is serialised execution, not encapsulation: a single-threaded context, or a dispatcher view whose parallelism is limited to one. Wrapping the fields in a class that exposes suspending functions achieves nothing by itself — two callers still enter those functions at the same time, on two threads, and race exactly as if they had touched the fields directly. The Kotlin guide is explicit about the granularity trap: confining each individual increment, so that every tiny mutation switches context, works very slowly, while confining a whole chunk of work to the owner is fast and still correct. The cost being paid is the context switch, so it should be paid once per body of work, not once per field write.

Confinement has a limit of its own, and it is the one that leads to the third mechanism. A serialised owner serialises execution, not a logical operation. The limitedParallelism KDoc makes the point itself: the limit is on how many coroutines execute at the same time, not on how many are inside the block, and it recommends a Mutex or Semaphore when what is wanted is mutual exclusion. If the owner suspends midway through an update, another coroutine can run on that context before it resumes.

A Mutex fits exactly that case: a critical section that must stay consistent across several steps, including suspending ones. Its defining property is that Mutex.lock() is a suspending function and does not block a thread, which is what makes it usable inside a coroutine at all. withLock is the structured form of lock, try, finally, unlock, so the lock is released even if the block throws or the coroutine is cancelled.

Protecting a line instead of an invariant. A lock taken around one statement, or an atomic per field, makes each individual write safe and still allows another coroutine to observe the state halfway through a change that was supposed to be one step.
Choosing between the three is a design decision before it is a performance one, and the shape of the state usually decides it.

rows: One independent value with a single-operation update
An atomic
A Mutex serialises a hot path for no benefit; confinement adds a context switch for one write.
Several related fields that must agree across a few steps
A Mutex around the critical section
Atomics protect each field and not the relationship; a serialised context does not hold across a suspension point inside the section.
A body of related state with a natural owner
Confinement to that owner
Locks spread the invariant across every call site that has to remember to take them.

blocks.text: The failure mode worth naming is reaching for a lock because code looked racy. A Mutex around a frequently taken path serialises it, and if the contention was imaginary the cost is not. The honest sequence is to establish that the state really is shared and really is mutable, choose the narrowest mechanism that protects the actual invariant, and then measure if the path matters. It is also worth asking whether the state needs to be shared at all: a value computed independently and returned is not a coordination problem, and a great deal of accidental sharing is really an ownership question that was never asked.

There is a fourth option that changes the question rather than answering it. Instead of making shared mutable state safe for everyone who touches it, coroutines can communicate: one coroutine owns the state and others send it values or commands, which is what a Channel is for. That is often the cleaner design when the alternative is several coroutines negotiating over one structure. The full comparison between passing values through a Channel and observing them through a stream belongs to the hot and cold streams material later in this curriculum; here it is enough to know the option exists and that share safely and communicate instead are different answers to the same problem.

items: A race needs concurrency and shared mutable state; removing either removes the race.
Read-modify-write is not atomic, and volatile fixes visibility rather than atomicity.
Common atomics exist in kotlin.concurrent.atomics behind an experimental opt-in, and are trivial on single-threaded targets.
An atomic protects one value; a Mutex protects an invariant across several steps.
Confinement means serialised execution rather than encapsulation, and it is coarse-grained or it is slow.
Mutex.lock() suspends rather than blocking, and withLock releases through failure and cancellation.

blocks.text: Given a counter incremented from many coroutines on a multi-threaded dispatcher, explain the wrong total in terms of read-modify-write. Then justify a choice among an atomic, a single owner and a Mutex for a given shape of state, and say when communication would be a better design than sharing.

units.title: Flow Fundamentals
units.summary: The first three units built a coroutine, gave it an owner, decided where it runs and worked out what happens when it stops or fails — and every one of those operations produced a single result. This unit asks the other question: what if the caller has to keep hearing about a value as it changes? Flow is the answer, and it is not a separate reactive world. A cold flow is a description of asynchronous production that runs inside an ordinary coroutine, ends when that coroutine ends, and is cancelled by the model the cancellation unit already taught. The order is one argument: why the shape exists, what cold means, who owns the collection, where it executes, and how an existing producer becomes a flow without leaking.

lessons.title: One Value or Many: Why `Flow` Exists
lessons.summary: Decide whether an operation should return one result or produce values over time. A suspending function answers a question once and then goes silent; a Flow-returning API keeps the caller in step with a changing value, and charges the caller collection, a coroutine, a lifetime and repeated delivery for it.

blocks.text: Everything the first three units built had the same shape at its edges. A caller asks for something, a coroutine suspends while the work happens, and an answer comes back: loadUser(id) returns a User, saveDraft(text) returns when the draft is saved. That shape is right for a great many operations. It is wrong for one specific situation, and the situation is common enough to have its own type.

Take a value that lives in local storage and can be written by more than one part of the app — the selected theme, say. A suspending read answers correctly at the moment it is called. Then something else writes a new theme: another screen, a sync job, a restore from backup. The suspending call has already returned. It has no way to say anything further, so the caller is now holding a value that used to be true.

Flow<T> is Kotlin's type for the second shape: a stream of values produced asynchronously, which a consumer receives one at a time. Notice what the two signatures promise. The suspending one promises an answer. The Flow-returning one is not a suspending function at all — it returns immediately, because it hands back a description of how values will be produced rather than any value. What that description does and when it runs is the next Lesson's subject; what matters here is that the two signatures are two different contracts with the caller.

One thing the type does not settle is how many values there will be. Flow<T> describes zero or more values produced asynchronously, so a flow is free to emit nothing, to emit once and complete, or to run until it is cancelled. observeTheme() keeps emitting because that is what the function is for, not because its return type compels it. Cardinality and freshness are the API's contract and the author owes the caller that contract in words; the type only says that values arrive over time rather than in a single return.

The reason a suspending function cannot do the observing job is not a missing feature that could be added. A suspending function has exactly one moment at which it communicates with its caller, and that is the moment it returns. After it returns there is no channel left open in either direction. The only way to learn about a later change is to call it again, which requires already knowing that something changed — which is the problem.

The question that chooses the shape is not “can this data change?”, because nearly all data can. It is “does this consumer need to be told when it changes?” A consumer that needs one answer now gets a suspending function. A consumer that must stay in step with a changing value gets a Flow.

Android's guidance for the data and business layers states the division as a rule: classes in those layers should expose suspend functions for one-shot calls and Flow to notify about data changes. It is worth reading as two halves rather than one recommendation, because the suspending half is a recommendation too. A repository that observes storage and a repository that performs an action are not in tension; most repositories do both.

The observable member is the interesting one because it moves work onto the caller. Reaching for it should be a decision, so it is worth being explicit about what the caller now has to reason about that it did not before.

items: It has to collect the flow. Nothing is produced until it does, so a Flow that is returned and never collected is a function that was never called.
Collection is a suspending operation, so it needs a coroutine, and the caller has to decide which one.
That coroutine's lifetime becomes the collection's lifetime, so the caller has acquired a lifetime it now owns.
Values may arrive more than once — how many and for how long is this API's contract rather than a guarantee of Flow<T> — so any code downstream that assumed a single delivery has to be re-read.
For an ordinary cold flow, every collector runs the producer again, so two collectors can mean two database reads.

blocks.text: So the honest comparison is not that Flow is the more powerful shape. It is that a Flow-returning API buys currency — the consumer is never holding a stale value — and pays for it in caller-side complexity. Where the consumer genuinely needs to be current, that is a good trade and the suspending version would be a bug. Where it does not — a one-time upload, a validation call, a payment — the suspending signature is the accurate one, and wrapping a single result in a Flow is a worse API rather than a more modern one, because it advertises a contract the operation does not have.

Turning “this data can change” into “this API returns a Flow”. Almost all persisted data can change. The test is the consumer: a screen that must repaint when another part of the app writes needs a stream, while a use case that computes a total once and hands it to a report does not, and giving it one makes every caller reason about collection, cancellation and repeated delivery for a value that arrives exactly once.

There is a third possibility worth naming so that it is not silently assumed. Some stream abstractions exist independently of any consumer: they are producing whether or not anyone is listening, a second consumer joins the one that is already running rather than starting another, and a value can be held for whoever arrives next. Kotlin has those, and choosing between them and an ordinary flow is a real decision — but nothing in this unit needs them, and they are the subject of the hot streams unit later in this curriculum. This unit is about the ordinary cold flow, which is what a repository-shaped API almost always returns.

It is worth knowing why cold is the right default there. themeChanges() is a description of how to observe storage, and a description costs nothing to hand out. The decisions about who runs it, when, and for how long belong to the caller, who is the only one who knows the lifetime it should be attached to. A repository that started producing on its own behalf would be starting work in a lifetime it does not own — which is the ownership argument the scope Lesson made about ad-hoc scopes, arriving from a different direction.

One architectural consequence is worth a sentence and no more, because the architecture curriculum owns it. This shape is what makes a single source of truth workable in practice: if one component owns a value and hands out an observable view of it, every consumer converges on the same value without anybody having to broadcast, and without two consumers being able to disagree. Observability is the property that makes that possible; how to structure the layers around it is somebody else's Lesson.

Expect “when would you return a Flow instead of a suspend function?” Answer from the consumer's need rather than the data's volatility. Name the concrete inability: a suspending function communicates once, at the moment it returns, so it cannot report a later change without being asked again, and asking again requires already knowing. Then give the cost unprompted — collection, a coroutine to collect in, a lifetime to own, possibly repeated emissions, and for a cold flow repeated execution of the producer. “Flow if the data can change” is the fashionable answer; naming the trade is the engineering one. If pressed further, add that Flow<T> itself promises only zero or more values over time, so how many and how fresh is something the API has to document.

lessons.title: Cold Flows: Producer, Collector and Operators
lessons.summary: Say exactly what runs, and when, for a given chain. A cold flow is a description: constructing it executes nothing, adding operators to it executes nothing, a terminal operator starts collection inside the collecting coroutine, and each new collector runs the producer again from the beginning.

blocks.text: The previous Lesson called a Flow a description of how values will be produced. This Lesson makes that precise, because it is the fact everything else in the unit depends on.

Ask what has happened by the time that line finishes. The answer is nothing. Nothing was printed, loadFirst was not called, and no value exists anywhere. Measured on this project's JVM target: after constructing exactly this shape, the producer block had run zero times. What the variable holds is the block itself, wrapped in an object that knows how to run it later.

The Kotlin documentation states the rule in two sentences that are worth memorising as a pair: the code block of a cold flow builder does not run until a collector collects it, and each new collector starts a new execution of the flow. The same page offers the image that makes it stick — a cold flow is like a recipe. Having the recipe is not having dinner, and two people cooking from it cook twice.

This is the line that starts something. collect is a suspending call, so it can only be written inside a coroutine, and it runs the producer block inside that coroutine — not somewhere else, not on a thread the flow arranged for itself. “producer starting” prints now, the two loads happen now, and collect does not return until the producer is finished.

Four words are worth fixing here because the rest of the curriculum uses them precisely. The producer is the code that generates values, and everything closer to it is upstream. The collector is the code that receives them, and everything closer to it is downstream. An emission is one value leaving the producer. Collection is the whole act of running the chain for one consumer.
Constructing a flow runs nothing. Adding operators to it runs nothing. A terminal operator such as collect is what starts the producer, and it starts it inside the collecting coroutine.
The second half of the rule — each new collector starts a new execution — is the half that shows up in production behaviour.

blocks.code:
val articles = flow {
    executions++
    emit(loadFeatured())
    emit(loadRecent())
}

articles.collect { }   // executions is now 1, two values delivered
articles.collect { }   // executions is now 2, the same two values again

blocks.text: Measured on this project's JVM target, a two-emission flow collected twice ran its producer twice and delivered its values twice over: 1, 2, 1, 2. Take that literally when the producer does real work. If it opens a database cursor, two collectors are two cursors; if it issues a request, two collectors are two requests. And because the producer only runs during a collection, the flow object itself stores nothing — there is no current value to read off it, and holding a reference to a Flow is not holding data.

Operators are what turn one flow into a chain, and they come in two kinds. The documentation's definitions are exact: intermediate operators return a new downstream flow that consumes values from upstream flows and applies an operation to them, while terminal operators trigger the execution of the flow pipeline by collecting an upstream flow.

The consequence is the one worth carrying, and the documentation states it outright: intermediate operators are themselves cold, so the returned flow does not start processing values until it is collected. Measured on this project's JVM target, a flow with a map applied to it and no terminal operator had run its producer zero times; the same chain after a single collect had run it once. Terminal operators are the ones that collect, and there are more of them than the ones a guide happens to name: collect and collectLatest; the operators that reduce a flow to a value, such as first, last, single, count, toList, toSet, fold and reduce; and launchIn, which collects in a scope you hand it. The list is not the thing to memorise — the signature is. An operator that returns another Flow is intermediate and has started nothing; one that suspends to give you a result, or launches a coroutine to produce it, has collected.

What each intermediate operator is actually for — which to reach for, how they interact with timing, how a chain combines two sources, what happens when the collector cannot keep up — is the flow composition unit later in this curriculum. Here they matter only as the thing that does not start a flow.

Reading a Flow-typed property as a value. val theme: Flow<Theme> holds no theme. It holds instructions for producing themes, and until something collects it nothing has been produced and nothing has been stored. Code that logs it, compares two of them, or expects reading the property to yield a current value is reasoning about the wrong object.

Kotlin's Sequence is the closest thing in the standard library, and the documentation makes the comparison itself: like sequences, cold flows are lazy. The shared idea is real and useful. A sequence performs all the processing steps one-by-one for every single element rather than completing each step for the whole collection and materialising an intermediate collection at each stage, and a flow chain behaves the same way — a value goes all the way down before the next one is produced.

Then stop, because the analogy has a hard edge, and the Flow documentation draws it in one clause: unlike in sequences, you can call suspending functions inside a flow builder. The sequences documentation, for its part, does not discuss coroutines at all. A Sequence produces its next value by returning from an ordinary function call, so the thread waits for it. A Flow produces its next value from a producer that can suspend, which is what lets an emission wait on a database, a socket or a timer without holding a thread. Flow is the asynchronous member of the pair, and everything in this unit that is interesting — collection lifetime, cancellation, execution context — follows from that one difference rather than from laziness.

The other limit worth stating is on the word cold itself. Cold is a property of this flow, not of the Flow type. Kotlin also has stream types whose production exists independently of collectors, where a second collector joins one running producer instead of starting a second, and where a value is held for whoever arrives next. Everything in this Lesson describes the cold case. Taking “each collector re-runs the producer” as a fact about Flow in general is exactly the mistake the hot streams unit later in this curriculum exists to correct, and the Compose bridge into flows linked below is another place the same cold model already shows up.

Three questions come out of this Lesson and they are asked about code rather than about definitions. Does constructing this flow execute anything? No, and neither does adding operators to it. What does a second collector cause? A second, independent execution of the producer from the beginning, with its own database read or its own request. What starts it? A terminal operator, which runs the producer inside the collecting coroutine. Being able to answer all three about a snippet you have not seen before is the model; the operator names can be looked up, this cannot.

lessons.title: Collection Lifetime and Flow Cancellation
lessons.summary: Name the coroutine a collection runs in, and what will end it. A cold flow has no lifetime of its own: collect runs the producer under the collecting coroutine, so that coroutine's Job bounds the collection and cancelling it is the ordinary cooperative cancellation Unit 3 already taught, not a Flow-specific mechanism.

blocks.text: Two questions are worth asking of any flow collection you read: which coroutine is this running in, and what will end it. The reason this Lesson comes fourth in the curriculum rather than first is that both answers are already known — they are the coroutine model of the first three units applied to a new shape, not new rules to learn.

A cold flow has no lifetime of its own. In the simplest pipeline — a flow { } builder collected directly — there is no second coroutine anywhere: the producer body runs inside the collecting coroutine. Some operators do introduce one, and this unit meets two of them later, where flowOn runs the upstream in its own coroutine and channelFlow launches children. What does not change is the ownership. Any coroutine a flow creates is a child of the collecting coroutine, created when collection starts and finished when it ends, so nothing a flow does is scheduled behind the collector's back or outlives it. The documentation puts that in two sentences: flow collection is tied to the coroutine that calls the collect() function, and when that coroutine is cancelled, the collection stops and the upstream flow is cancelled too.

Everything follows from the second line running inside the first. The producer executes in this coroutine, in its context, under its Job, which is a child of the scope's Job. collect suspends and does not return until the flow completes or the coroutine is cancelled — and a flow that observes storage never completes on its own, so in practice cancellation is how collection ends.

That turns a scheduling question into an ownership question. Choosing where to collect is choosing who owns the collection's lifetime, because the scope you launch it in is the thing that will eventually end it. A collection launched in a screen's scope lasts as long as the screen; a collection launched in an application-lifetime scope lasts as long as the process, whether or not anything is still interested.

There is no such thing as “the flow's lifetime”. There is the collecting coroutine's lifetime, and the collection is part of it. Deciding which scope collects is therefore the whole of the lifetime decision.

Collection is often written the other way round, and the shorthand is worth reading carefully because it is frequently misdescribed. The KDoc says exactly what it is: launchIn is a terminal flow operator that launches the collection of the given flow in a scope, and it is a shorthand for scope.launch { flow.collect() }.

Two things about it are precise. It is a terminal operator, so it is the thing that starts the flow — onEach is an ordinary intermediate operator and would do nothing on its own. And it returns a Job, the same handle the Job Lesson introduced, which means the collection is an ordinary child coroutine of that scope with an ordinary lifetime. Measured on this project's JVM target, launchIn returned a StandaloneCoroutine which is a Job, and cancelling the scope ended the collection it had started.

What launchIn does not do is change the flow's contract. It does not make a cold flow hot: the source still produces per collection, and two launchIn calls on the same cold flow are two collections. Measured on this project's JVM target, the same cold adapter collected through two launchIn calls executed its producer twice, exactly as two plain collect calls would. The KDoc's own note points the same way — the provided scope takes care of cancellation, and the returned Job does not need to be used for cancellation purposes, because the scope is the owner.

Where that scope comes from is an application question rather than a Flow question. UI applications generally collect in a scope bound to the lifetime of whatever is displaying the values, so that navigating away ends the collection. The lifecycle-aware ways of arranging that, and the Compose-side ways of collecting a flow into state, are the subject of the effects and lifecycle integration material later in this curriculum; the mechanism underneath every one of them is the one this Lesson describes.

Collecting in a scope that outlives the consumer. The collection is not aware of who wanted the values: if the coroutine is still alive, the producer keeps running, the database keeps being read and the results go nowhere. Nothing about this fails loudly, which is what makes choosing the scope a correctness decision rather than a tidiness one.

“Cancelling the collector cancels the upstream flow” is true and is also the sentence most likely to be over-read. Unit 3's model is unchanged here, and Flow does not introduce a second one: cancellation is a request recorded on a Job, and the code inside stops where it can observe that request. A producer does not become forcibly interruptible by virtue of sitting inside a flow.

Measured on this project's JVM target, with a producer whose first statement was a six-hundred-millisecond blocking sleep — a JVM-specific case, used here because it is the clearest one — the collecting coroutine was cancelled after a hundred milliseconds. The blocking call ran to completion anyway, and joining the cancelled coroutine returned six hundred and ninety-four milliseconds after the start. The producer was inside a flow, it had been cancelled, and it was still not interruptible.

The ordinary case is much better behaved, and for a documented reason: the flow builder is cancellable by default, which means cancellation is checked on each emission, and on top of that almost everything a realistic producer does between emissions is itself a suspending call. Measured on this project's JVM target with a producer whose only cooperative point was emit — a tight loop with no delay, no yield and no other suspending call anywhere in it — cancelling the collector stopped it: the loop never exited normally and the coroutine completed. So the accurate formulation is the one Unit 3 already gave. Cancelling the collector requests cancellation of production, and production stops where it observes the request; in a flow built the ordinary way, that is almost immediately, and the only producers that overrun are the ones doing work that cooperates with nothing.

Notice what is absent from that formulation. There is no Flow-specific kill switch, no separate collection lifecycle, and no Job the flow owns independently of its collector — the child coroutines some operators create are exactly that, children, and they are cancelled through the ordinary hierarchy. This is worth stating explicitly because the alternative mental model, that a flow is a live thing with its own lifecycle that cancellation reaches into, leads to exactly the wrong predictions about non-cooperative producers and about who is responsible for stopping what.

Be ready for the pair. Which coroutine owns this collection, and what ends it? The one that called collect, and cancelling it — usually by cancelling the scope it belongs to. Does launchIn make the flow hot? No; it is scope.launch { collect() } and returns a Job, and the source's cold contract is untouched. Then add the precision that separates a careful answer from a slogan: cancelling a collector cancels production cooperatively, so a producer doing non-cooperative work will finish it, and the caller waits.

lessons.title: Context Preservation and `flowOn`
lessons.summary: Say which part of a chain runs in which context. A cold flow runs in the collector's context by default, an ordinary flow { } producer may not switch its own emission context, and flowOn exists precisely because of that rule — it moves the upstream and leaves the collector where it was.

blocks.text: The previous Lesson settled who owns a collection. This one settles where it runs, and the answer is again borrowed rather than new: Unit 2's context model applies unchanged, because a cold flow executes inside the collecting coroutine and therefore in the collecting coroutine's context.

The documentation states the default in one sentence: by default, a cold flow runs in the same coroutine context as the collector. Nothing about writing flow { } selects a dispatcher, and nothing about a value being asynchronous moves it off the caller's thread.

This is the same misconception Unit 1 removed about the suspend keyword, arriving in new clothing. A suspending function does not run in the background because it is suspending, and a flow does not run in the background because it is a flow. If the collection is on a UI dispatcher, so is the file read, and the screen will show it.

The property has a name — a flow is context-preserving — and the reason it is worth having is that it makes a chain locally readable. When you look at a collect call, the context that the whole chain executes in is the context you are looking at, unless an operator in front of you says otherwise. No operator halfway up the chain can quietly change the answer.

A cold flow has no context of its own. It runs in the collector's context, so “where does this flow run?” is always answered by reading the collector and then reading the operators between the collector and the producer.

Which raises the obvious question: if the file read should not happen on the UI dispatcher, why not move it inside the producer, where the work actually is? Because that is exactly what a flow may not do.

The flow builder's KDoc states the requirement — emit should happen strictly in the dispatchers of the block in order to preserve the flow context — and carries this exact case as its own illustration of an IllegalStateException. Run it against the coroutines version this repository resolves and the runtime explains itself:

blocks.code:
IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated:
	Flow was collected in [CoroutineId(1), "coroutine#1":BlockingCoroutine{Active}@..., BlockingEventLoop@...],
	but emission happened in [CoroutineId(1), "coroutine#1":DispatchedCoroutine{Active}@..., Dispatchers.IO].
	Please refer to 'flow' documentation or use 'flowOn' instead

blocks.text: The message names the two contexts it compared and then names the remedy, which is the useful part. The rule is not bureaucratic: if a producer could switch its own emission context, a reader of a collect call could no longer know which context their collection runs in without tracing every operator back to the source, and the local readability the previous section described would be gone. Preserving the context is what keeps the local reading correct — and flowOn is the sanctioned way to change it.

blocks.code:
fileLines()                    // runs in ioDispatcher
    .map { parse(it) }         // runs in ioDispatcher
    .flowOn(ioDispatcher)
    .collect { render(it) }    // runs in the collector's context, untouched

blocks.text: The direction is the entire operator, and the KDoc says it plainly: flowOn is context preserving, context does not leak into the downstream flow, and it affects only preceding operators that do not have their own context. Upstream moves; downstream, including the terminal collector, stays exactly where it was.

That makes placement a decision rather than a ritual. Moving flowOn changes which operators are above it and therefore which ones move, and a chain may carry more than one — the KDoc's own worked example uses two, each governing the operators between itself and the one before it. The question to ask is never “where does flowOn go” but “which upstream work needs a different execution context”. If the answer is none, the operator does not belong in the chain at all.

Reading flowOn(ioDispatcher) as “this flow runs on IO”. It says that the operators above it do. The collector and everything below it stay where they were, which is usually precisely what is wanted: parse off the UI dispatcher, render on it. A reader who has the direction backwards will also put the operator in the wrong place.

It is worth knowing what changing the context actually costs, because flowOn does more than relabel the upstream. When the dispatcher changes, the KDoc says, the flow's emissions are performed in a coroutine running with the specified context and the values are collected in another coroutine using the original collector's context, with a channel of default buffer size used internally between the two. Two coroutines and a channel — which is how the invariant can be honoured at all, since the producer really is emitting in its own context and something else really is receiving in the collector's.

The side effect of that arrangement is that flowOn introduces concurrency and buffering as well as a context change: the upstream can run ahead of the collector up to the buffer's capacity. What to do when a producer outpaces its collector is the buffering material in the flow composition unit later in this curriculum. Here it is enough to know that the operator is not free and is not purely declarative.

Unit 2's precision about context and threads carries forward unchanged, and this operator is a good place to see why it mattered. Measured on this project's JVM target: a chain whose upstream was moved with flowOn(Dispatchers.IO), collected from a coroutine already running on Dispatchers.Default. The upstream did run in a separate coroutine, as the KDoc describes — but the thread it landed on was named DefaultDispatcher-worker-3, and the collector's was DefaultDispatcher-worker-1. Asking for IO did not produce a thread from some separate IO pool, because there is no separate pool: the Dispatchers.IO reference states that it shares threads with Default, and that switching to it when already on Default typically does not lead to an actual switch to another thread. What flowOn guarantees is about the context. Which physical thread that turns into is a scheduling detail, and reasoning that depends on a particular one is folklore.

One last connection, named rather than taught. Context preservation is one instance of a more general transparency rule rather than a quirk of flowOn: just as a producer may not change the context its emissions happen in, an operator may not silently swallow a failure that belongs to code downstream of it. The operators that let a chain observe and transform failures are built to keep that boundary intact, and they are the subject of the failure material in the flow composition unit later in this curriculum.

Two questions, and the second is the better one. Which operators does flowOn affect? Everything upstream of it and nothing downstream, the collector included. And why is withContext around emit inside flow { } wrong? Because a flow is context-preserving, so that a collector can know its own execution context by reading its own code, and the runtime enforces it with an IllegalStateException whose message names flowOn as the remedy. The first question asks what the operator does; the second asks why it exists, which is what the invariant is actually for.

lessons.title: Flow Builders and Adapting Callback APIs
lessons.summary: Turn an existing producer into a flow without leaking it. The producer's shape picks the builder: sequential suspending work is flow, several coroutines producing at once is channelFlow, and a callback or listener API is callbackFlow — where awaitClose is what keeps the registration alive and gives unregistration one place that always runs.

blocks.text: Every flow so far has come from flow { }, which fits producers of one particular shape: sequential work, done by suspending calls, emitting from the builder's own coroutine.

Nothing about that builder limits how many values are produced or how long production takes. What it does limit is where emission may happen, which is the rule the previous Lesson established: emission has to occur in the builder's own context, from the builder's own coroutine. Two perfectly ordinary producers do not fit inside that rule, and Kotlin supplies a builder for each of them.

The first is work done concurrently by several coroutines. channelFlow allows elements to be produced by code that is running in a different context or concurrently, and it ensures thread-safety and context preservation, so its ProducerScope can be used concurrently from different contexts. Inside it, send replaces emit.

It is still a cold flow — the KDoc is explicit that the block is called every time a terminal operator is applied to the resulting flow — and what it buys is concurrency, at the price of ordering. Measured on this project's JVM target, a channelFlow with two child coroutines, one of them delayed, delivered its values in the order they were actually produced rather than the order the children were launched. That is the builder working as intended, and it is the reason to reach for it deliberately rather than by default.

The builder follows from the producer's shape rather than from preference. Sequential suspending production is flow. Production by several coroutines at once is channelFlow. A callback or listener belonging to something outside the coroutine world is callbackFlow.

The second producer that does not fit flow { } is the important one in practice, because the world outside coroutines is full of register-and-be-called-back APIs: sensors, location, connectivity, players, sockets, platform observers. Adapting one into a flow is the most common flow-authoring job there is, and it is the one with a leak built into the obvious version.

Read that block as a lifetime rather than as a snippet. Registration happens when a collection starts. trySend moves each value from whatever thread the callback arrived on into the flow's channel, which is why a plain flow { } cannot be used here at all: the callback is not running in the builder's coroutine, and emitting from it would violate the context invariant the previous Lesson described. And then the block reaches awaitClose, which is where the interesting part is.

The one thing worth adding to that line is what happens when trySend does not succeed. A callback is not a coroutine, so trySend cannot suspend and cannot apply back pressure the way emit does; it attempts the send and hands back a result. That result is a failure when the channel's buffer is full or when collection has already ended, and ignoring it means the adapter silently loses values. Which is sometimes exactly right — for a position that will be superseded a moment later, dropping is the correct policy — but it should be a decision the adapter states rather than a consequence of not looking. Inspect the result and do something honest with it: record the drop, count it, or surface it. Choosing a buffering policy instead is the subject named at the end of this Lesson.

Without awaitClose the block would return the instant the listener was registered, the channel would close, and the collection would end — with the listener still attached to the source. The library refuses to let that happen silently. Its KDoc says awaitClose should be used to keep the flow running, that otherwise the channel will be closed immediately when the block completes, and that using it is mandatory in order to prevent memory leaks. Measured on this project's JVM target, a callbackFlow whose block sent one value and returned failed with:

blocks.code:
IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end
of callbackFlow block. Otherwise, a callback/listener may leak in case of external cancellation.
See callbackFlow API documentation for the details.

blocks.text: The failure it is protecting against is concrete rather than theoretical. The listener stays registered; the source keeps a reference to it and to everything the listener captured, which in a UI application is frequently a screen that has already gone; and it keeps being invoked to deliver values to a consumer that no longer exists. awaitClose closes that hole by construction: it suspends until the channel is closed or cancelled, and its block is executed unconditionally before the function returns — the same guarantee a finally block gives, which is exactly the shape the cleanup Lesson taught.

Registering in the callbackFlow block and unregistering somewhere else — a lifecycle callback, a close() method, a disposal hook. The registration belongs to this collection, and awaitClose is the one place that runs when this collection ends, however it ends. Splitting the pair across two files is how a listener survives the thing that created it.

Because a callbackFlow is cold, each collection registers its own listener. Measured on this project's JVM target, one adapter collected by two coroutines registered twice while both were running, and when the scope was cancelled it unregistered twice. That is usually the behaviour you want — each consumer owns its own subscription and its own cleanup, and no consumer can end another's — but it is a genuine cost when registration is expensive, or when the underlying source only tolerates one listener. The remedy is not a different builder; it is sharing one collection among several consumers, which is the subject of the hot streams unit later in this curriculum.
With that, the choice among the three builders can be stated as reasoning rather than as a lookup table.

rows: A sequence of suspending calls made by one coroutine
flow
The simplest contract that works, and the one that keeps context preservation checkable. Nothing more is needed, so nothing more should be paid for.
Several coroutines producing values at the same time
channelFlow
Emission from more than one coroutine needs the thread-safe, context-preserving channel this builder supplies. Ordering is given up in exchange.
A callback or listener registered against an external source
callbackFlow
Values arrive outside any coroutine, and the registration needs a lifetime boundary that runs on cancellation — which is what awaitClose is.

blocks.text: The last two are not interchangeable, even though both are built on the same channel-backed producer scope. channelFlow answers a question about who is allowed to produce; callbackFlow answers a question about a subscription that has to be torn down. Reaching for channelFlow around a listener leaves you writing awaitClose anyway, without the builder's insistence that you did; reaching for callbackFlow around ordinary concurrent work names a callback that does not exist. And note what neither is: the channel is an implementation detail of the builder, and channels as a coordination primitive in their own right — capacities, fan-out, pipelines — are a separate subject this unit deliberately leaves alone.

One consequence of that implementation detail is worth naming before leaving it. Both builders use a channel with the default buffer size, so a producer that runs ahead of its collector is buffered rather than immediately suspended, and trySend returns a result that can report failure when the buffer is full or the channel is already closed. Deciding what should happen when a producer outpaces its collector — buffer more, drop values, cancel work in flight — is the buffering material in the flow composition unit later in this curriculum.

This Lesson's interview version is short and unusually specific. Which builder adapts a listener API? callbackFlow. Why must the block end in awaitClose? Because the block returns as soon as the listener is registered, so awaitClose is what keeps the collection alive while callbacks may still arrive and gives unregistration one place that runs however the collection ends — and the builder throws IllegalStateException if it is missing. Who unregisters, and when? The awaitClose block, when the collecting coroutine is cancelled or the channel closes. Then the question that separates having used it from having read about it: does a cold adapter create one subscription or one per collection? One per collection.
